title: Fact-Checking President Tshisekedi’s Address at the Global Gateway Forum 2025 in Brussels
excerpt: Brussels, October 9, 2025 -During his address at the Global Gateway Forum 2025, Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) President Félix Tshisekedi delivered a speech calling for peace and regional cooperation, particularly…
title_en: Fact-Checking President Tshisekedi’s Address at the Global Gateway Forum 2025 in Brussels
excerpt_en: Brussels, October 9, 2025 -During his address at the Global Gateway Forum 2025, Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) President Félix Tshisekedi delivered a speech calling for peace and regional cooperation, particularly…
body_en:
Brussels, October 9, 2025 -During his address at the Global Gateway Forum 2025, Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) President Félix Tshisekedi delivered a speech calling for peace and regional cooperation, particularly with neighboring Rwanda and Uganda. However, a closer examination of his statements reveals several inconsistencies with facts and recent developments in the region.

Claim 1: “Since I was elected in 2019, I have visited all nine neighbouring countries, particularly Rwanda and Uganda, to propose working together for development and well-being.”

While it is true that President Tshisekedi initiated diplomatic visits to several neighboring states early in his tenure, relations with Rwanda and Uganda have since deteriorated sharply.Since 1999, more than ten peace agreements have been signed between the DRC and its neighbors but rarely implemented - largely due to Kinshasa’s preference for military solutions and persistent political mistrust.

Analysts also point to anti-Rwandan rhetoric and internal persecution of certain Congolese communities, notably Congolese Tutsi, which has intensified in recent years under Tshisekedi’s administration.

Claim 2: “At no time have I displayed any belligerent attitude towards Rwanda or Uganda.”

This statement contradicts numerous public speeches and interviews in which President Tshisekedi used hostile language toward Rwanda and its leadership.During his 2023 re-election campaign, Tshisekedi referred to Rwandan President Paul Kagame as “Hitler”, threatened to “bomb Kigali,” and vowed to “work with Rwanda’s enemies.”

Such rhetoric has also echoed in regional and international fora, where DRC officials have repeatedly accused Rwanda of backing the M23 rebellion and called for sanctions against Kigali.Locally, Congolese officials have often blamed domestic challenges - from corruption scandals to economic stagnation - on Rwanda, fueling anti-Rwanda sentiment and hate speech within the country.

Claim 3: “We are the only two capable of stopping this escalation.”

Observers argue that escalation largely depends on Kinshasa’s decisions, particularly regarding the FDLR militia, a Rwandan rebel group based in eastern Congo and accused of participating in the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi. Despite regional commitments through the EAC, AU, and SADC, the DRC has continued to collaborate with FDLR units, foreign mercenaries, and local militias such as the Wazalendo, worsening instability. Rwanda maintains that peace can only be achieved through direct dialogue between the DRC government and AFC/M23, a Congolese rebel movement involved in the Doha peace process.

Claim 4: “Rwanda boycotted a near-final peace ceremony for no reason.”

Rwanda’s government publicly stated that it refused to participate in the Luanda ceremony because the DRC failed to honor prior commitments, including talks with internal rebel movements. Kigali described the event as a “photo opportunity” that did not address core security issues.

Claim 5: “M23 must stop its escalation supported by Rwanda.”

The DRC government continues to blame Rwanda for supporting the M23, a claim Kigali denies.Independent observers and regional mediators, however, note that Kinshasa’s own actions - such as the failure to demobilize the FDLR and recruitment of foreign mercenaries - have equally fueled the conflict.

Multiple cross-border incidents have been recorded since 2019, including artillery shelling in January 2025 that killed at least 16 Rwandan civilians in Rubavu District.

Claim 6: “We have been counting them in the millions for years.”

Tshisekedi’s reference to “millions” of victims has no verified statistical basis. While the humanitarian toll of the eastern Congo conflict is indeed catastrophic, experts caution against politically motivated exaggerations that distort the scope of the crisis.

Claim 7: “We remain grateful to SADC troops who fell on the field of honour.”

SADC forces, deployed in late 2024 to support the Congolese army, suffered heavy losses during clashes in North Kivu. Following the fall of Goma, surviving troops and foreign mercenaries were reportedly granted safe passage through Rwanda after withdrawal.

Claim 8: “The DRC is not belligerent and wants peace.”

Despite Tshisekedi’s final appeal for peace, his government’s ongoing military offensives, hate-driven narratives, and failure to implement regional peace accords contradict this claim.Analysts and regional mediators stress that peace will only come from sincere political will - notably, through dismantling the FDLR, ceasing anti-Rwanda provocations, and re-engaging in Doha and Luanda peace mechanisms in good faith.

President Tshisekedi’s speech in Brussels projected an image of a leader committed to peace and dialogue. However, a detailed fact-check reveals a pattern of contradictions between his public statements and the DRC’s actions on the ground. While the DRC continues to frame itself as a victim of external aggression, evidence points to internal political choices, military miscalculations, and regional defiance as major obstacles to peace in the Great Lakes region.

title: Kagame’s Spokesperson Condemns Tshisekedi’s Remarks at Brussels Forum
excerpt: BRUSSELS - Stéphanie Nyombayire, spokesperson for the Office of the President of Rwanda, has sharply criticized Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) President Félix Antoine Tshisekedi, accusing him of hypocrisy and…
title_en: Kagame’s Spokesperson Condemns Tshisekedi’s Remarks at Brussels Forum
excerpt_en: BRUSSELS - Stéphanie Nyombayire, spokesperson for the Office of the President of Rwanda, has sharply criticized Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) President Félix Antoine Tshisekedi, accusing him of hypocrisy and…
body_en:
BRUSSELS - Stéphanie Nyombayire, spokesperson for the Office of the President of Rwanda, has sharply criticized Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) President Félix Antoine Tshisekedi, accusing him of hypocrisy and irresponsibility in fueling tensions between the two countries.

Speaking on October 9, 2025, following Tshisekedi’s address at the Global Gateway Forum 2025 in Brussels, Nyombayire said she was “disappointed” that the Congolese leader used an international economic platform to attack Rwanda rather than engage constructively.

During his speech, Tshisekedi blamed Rwanda for strained relations with the DRC, while avoiding acknowledgment of his own role in the escalating crisis. In response, Nyombayire took to X (formerly Twitter), describing his comments as “shameless” and “deeply misleading.”

title: AFC/M23 Warns DRC: “No Escaping the Doha Peace Talks”
excerpt: The AFC/M23 coalition has urged the government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) to fully commit to the ongoing peace talks in Doha, warning that they remain the only viable path to ending the protracted…
title_en: AFC/M23 Warns DRC: “No Escaping the Doha Peace Talks”
excerpt_en: The AFC/M23 coalition has urged the government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) to fully commit to the ongoing peace talks in Doha, warning that they remain the only viable path to ending the protracted…
body_en:
The AFC/M23 coalition has urged the government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) to fully commit to the ongoing peace talks in Doha, warning that they remain the only viable path to ending the protracted conflict in eastern Congo.

The negotiations, mediated by the Qatari government since March 2025, have struggled to produce tangible results, with several key issues still unresolved. After being suspended earlier this year, the talks resumed in July, leading to partial progress as both sides agreed on guiding principles toward a lasting peace.

Despite these advances, implementation has stalled. Fighting in North Kivu and surrounding areas continues, undermining expectations that hostilities would cease following initial commitments.

In a message published on X, the AFC/M23 referenced recent meetings between U.S. Presidential Advisor on Africa, Massad Boulos, and Presidents Félix Tshisekedi of the DRC and Paul Kagame of Rwanda. According to the group, discussions focused primarily on the U.S.-brokered peace initiative and the resumption of the Doha process.

“The Doha talks are not merely a platform for dialogue but a genuine path to peace,” the AFC/M23 statement read. “Both parties must build mutual trust, release political prisoners, halt hostilities, and fully adhere to the agreed principles.”

The group further stressed that, as the talks prepare to reconvene for a sixth time, Kinshasa must participate “with mutual respect and equality.”

“The government has previously attempted to avoid these discussions,” the statement continued. “But in Doha, there is no superior or subordinate side-both parties sit at the same table to discuss the same nation, the Democratic Republic of Congo.”

AFC/M23 also warned that the broader U.S.-supported peace framework, particularly regarding the management of Congo’s mineral resources, cannot move forward without meaningful progress in the Doha negotiations.

title: Nyamasheke Launches Construction of 21-Kilometer Road to Connect Three Isolated Sectors
excerpt: The Nyamasheke District administration has begun construction of the 21-kilometer Bushenge-Shangi-Nyabitekeri road, a long-awaited project aimed at easing transportation, boosting trade, and ending the isolation of…
title_en: Nyamasheke Launches Construction of 21-Kilometer Road to Connect Three Isolated Sectors
excerpt_en: The Nyamasheke District administration has begun construction of the 21-kilometer Bushenge-Shangi-Nyabitekeri road, a long-awaited project aimed at easing transportation, boosting trade, and ending the isolation of…
body_en:
The Nyamasheke District administration has begun construction of the 21-kilometer Bushenge-Shangi-Nyabitekeri road, a long-awaited project aimed at easing transportation, boosting trade, and ending the isolation of residents in three sectors along Lake Kivu.

Bushenge, Shangi, and Nyabitekeri are among ten sectors in Nyamasheke District that border Lake Kivu and have long struggled with poor accessibility due to the deteriorated road linking them to the main Kivu asphalt route.

Local residents have welcomed the project, hoping it will ease their daily travel and reduce transportation costs.Dan Nkurunziza, a project manager working in Nyabitekeri Sector, told IGIHE that residents currently pay as much as 16,000 Rwandan francs for a round trip to nearby areas.

“We are happy that this road is finally under construction-it will reduce travel costs. Once completed, public transport vehicles that stopped operating here will return, and residents will no longer be cut off,” Nkurunziza said.

The road is also expected to improve access to Bushenge Hospital, which serves the three sectors. Previously, heavy rains often made it impossible to transport patients, as the road became impassable during the rainy season.

Nyamasheke District Mayor, Mupenzi Narcisse, confirmed that construction is underway, with three contractors assigned to accelerate the project.

“The road, which runs from Bushenge Hospital to Nyamirundi, will be built as a feeder road with strong foundations, bridges, and drainage systems,” Mupenzi said. “It will facilitate communication, improve trade, and enhance agricultural productivity.”

The mayor added that upon completion, the road is expected to significantly boost local economic activity by easing the transport of agricultural produce to the main Kivu asphalt road.

The project is scheduled to be completed within one year and eight months at a total cost of over 8 billion Rwandan francs.

title: U.S. welcomes DRC call for FDLR to disarm, urges orderly surrender under Washington agreement
excerpt: The United States on Friday welcomed a decision by the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) calling on fighters of the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) to lay down their arms and surrender to either…
title_en: U.S. welcomes DRC call for FDLR to disarm, urges orderly surrender under Washington agreement
excerpt_en: The United States on Friday welcomed a decision by the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) calling on fighters of the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) to lay down their arms and surrender to either…
body_en:
The United States on Friday welcomed a decision by the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) calling on fighters of the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) to lay down their arms and surrender to either Congolese authorities or the United Nations peacekeeping mission, MONUSCO. The U.S. reaction framed the move as a key step in implementing the Washington peace agreement signed by Kinshasa and Kigali on June 27, 2025.

A statement issued by the DRC Armed Forces (FARDC) and signed by Major General Sylvain Ekenge Bomusa on October 10, 2025, urged FDLR fighters to disarm and surrender “to the government or MONUSCO.” The military message said the order follows an operational directive adopted on October 1 and reiterated that FARDC personnel are forbidden from cooperating with the FDLR in any form. It also warned that the FARDC “will disarm by force” those who refuse to lay down arms.

U.S. Senior Advisor on Africa Massad Boulos echoed those calls on X, describing Kinshasa’s directive as “a major step in the implementation of the Washington Peace Agreement.” Boulos said the move would facilitate the transfer of refugees, consolidate government authority, and bolster regional efforts to restore peace and security in the Great Lakes region. His post said the DRC’s announcement aligns with provisions of the June 27 accord that envisage the neutralization of the FDLR and related security measures monitored by a Joint Security Coordination Mechanism.

Why the DRC move matters - and why it is complicated

The Washington agreement between the DRC and Rwanda commits both countries to a package of steps including cessation of hostilities, disengagement of forces, and a harmonized plan to neutralize the FDLR. The Joint Security Coordination Mechanism (JSCM) created under that deal is tasked with overseeing aspects of the FDLR neutralization and other security provisions. International backers - led by the United States - have made implementation of those provisions central to the broader push for stability.

But convincing FDLR elements to disarm - and ensuring they do so without fueling further violence - will be difficult. United Nations and independent reporting over recent years has documented complex and sometimes opaque ties between some FDLR elements and Congolese armed groups, including allegations that former FDLR combatants or sympathizers have embedded in local militias or obtained protection from elements within the FARDC. Those overlapping loyalties, and the presence of rival armed formations such as the so-called “Wazalendo” groups, complicate identification and separation of genuine FDLR combatants from other fighters.

Questions of verification, protection and political will

Observers say three practical challenges will determine whether the DRC’s call leads to meaningful disarmament rather than a brief public relations gesture:

Verification: Who will verify that those surrendering are bona fide FDLR fighters and not members of other groups or irregulars attempting to avoid accountability? The JSCM and MONUSCO have roles to play, but their access and acceptance on the ground will be essential.

Security for surrendering combatants: Disarmament programs usually require guarantees on how former fighters will be treated - repatriation, demobilization, reintegration, or prosecution. The Washington agreement sketches a framework but does not eliminate the practical risks fighters fear if they give up arms.

Domestic enforcement: The FARDC’s own conduct will be scrutinized. The new military directive forbids cooperation with the FDLR, but critics note past instances where lines were blurred - making consistent enforcement critical to credibility.

Washington’s public support for Kinshasa’s call signals continued U.S. investment in the Washington process and in mechanisms - such as the JSCM - expected to monitor implementation. U.S. officials have tied political and technical support for the region to tangible progress on neutralizing the FDLR and reducing cross-border security risks. Reuters, AP and U.S. State Department material released around the June 27 signing likewise framed the deal as a package that links security, political confidence-building and regional economic cooperation.

The DRC’s October 10 directive - and U.S. endorsement - mark a potential turning point in the Washington-led push to address one of the most intractable armed groups in the eastern DRC. Yet success will depend on careful, credible verification, protections for surrendering fighters, and a demonstrable, consistent break between elements of the FARDC and armed proxies. Without those safeguards, the order could struggle to produce the disarmament and stabilization its authors envision.

title: Boris Johnson Urges UK to Revive Rwanda Deportation Plan Amid Debate Over New ID Card System
excerpt: Former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson has urged the British government to reinstate the controversial Rwanda deportation program for undocumented migrants, saying that new plans to introduce electronic ID cards will be…
title_en: Boris Johnson Urges UK to Revive Rwanda Deportation Plan Amid Debate Over New ID Card System
excerpt_en: Former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson has urged the British government to reinstate the controversial Rwanda deportation program for undocumented migrants, saying that new plans to introduce electronic ID cards will be…
body_en:
Former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson has urged the British government to reinstate the controversial Rwanda deportation program for undocumented migrants, saying that new plans to introduce electronic ID cards will be costly and ineffective in curbing illegal immigration.

In an interview with GB News, Johnson criticized Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s proposal to issue digital identity cards - including to children as young as 13 - as part of efforts to tighten immigration controls. The government argues that the cards, which would store extensive personal data, will allow authorities, employers, and landlords to easily verify the legal status of individuals living in the UK.

Starmer’s Labour government says the initiative forms part of a broader strategy to reduce irregular migration, combining enhanced border technology and stricter enforcement measures.

But Johnson, who led the government from 2019 to 2022, dismissed the plan as “an expensive distraction.” He argued that reinstating the Rwanda deportation scheme - suspended by Starmer shortly after taking office in July 2024 - would be a far more effective deterrent.

“If we had the Rwanda programme, we wouldn’t have let them score a goal. It would have been a back-and-forth move,” Johnson said, likening the flow of migrants across the English Channel to a football match.

Johnson’s Conservative government first signed the UK-Rwanda Migration and Economic Development Partnership in April 2022, under which asylum seekers who entered Britain illegally could be relocated to Rwanda for processing and potential resettlement. In return, Rwanda would receive financial support to facilitate their accommodation and reintegration.

The plan, however, faced immediate legal challenges. The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) halted the first scheduled deportation flight in June 2022, following complaints from human rights groups. Despite revisions and renewed bilateral commitments in late 2023 - including approval by both Houses of Parliament - the programme remained stalled.

When Starmer took office in mid-2024, his government formally suspended the Rwanda scheme, arguing that it failed to deter illegal crossings and raised serious human rights concerns.

Home Office figures show that 29,437 undocumented migrants entered the UK in 2023, a number that climbed to 43,640 in 2024. Between January and September 2025, the total reached 33,556, underscoring the continued challenge of managing irregular migration across the Channel.

Johnson’s comments have reignited debate over the future of Britain’s asylum and immigration policies - with some Conservative MPs backing a return to the Rwanda plan, while Labour insists its digital ID strategy represents a “fairer, more practical” long-term solution.

title: Tshisekedi and Minister Kayikwamba Clash Over Rwanda Policy at EU-AU Summit
excerpt: A diplomatic rift has emerged within the Congolese leadership after Foreign Minister Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner appeared to contradict President Félix Tshisekedi’s call for reconciliation with Rwanda during the European…
title_en: Tshisekedi and Minister Kayikwamba Clash Over Rwanda Policy at EU-AU Summit
excerpt_en: A diplomatic rift has emerged within the Congolese leadership after Foreign Minister Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner appeared to contradict President Félix Tshisekedi’s call for reconciliation with Rwanda during the European…
body_en:
A diplomatic rift has emerged within the Congolese leadership after Foreign Minister Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner appeared to contradict President Félix Tshisekedi’s call for reconciliation with Rwanda during the European Union-African Union Global Gateway Summit held on October 9, 2025, in Brussels.

During his address, President Tshisekedi declared that he had chosen dialogue over sanctions in dealing with Rwanda, signaling a softer tone in a relationship marked by years of mutual accusations over the conflict in eastern DRC.

“I had planned to request sanctions, but I decided to postpone them, waiting for President Kagame’s response,” Tshisekedi said, emphasizing his desire for “peaceful coexistence” between Kinshasa and Kigali.

He added that reconciliation would only be possible if Rwandan President Paul Kagame urged the M23 rebel movement to cease hostilities in North Kivu. Kigali has consistently denied any support for the rebel group, which remains active near the Congolese border.

Shortly after the summit, Foreign Minister Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner gave an interview to EUobserver, where she strongly criticized Rwanda, accusing it of backing the M23 and expressing “deep disappointment” over the European Union’s failure to impose sanctions on Kigali.

Her remarks appeared to directly contradict President Tshisekedi’s reconciliatory message, sparking confusion over the DRC government’s official position.

In response, Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, condemned Kayikwamba’s comments, calling them inconsistent with her president’s tone in Brussels.

“Minister Kayikwamba’s statements contradict President Tshisekedi’s call for reconciliation,” Nduhungirehe said. “They show that what Kinshasa calls ‘peace efforts’ are nothing more than a political performance for the media.”

He further noted that President Kagame had recently signed, alongside European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, a €95 million partnership agreement to support BioNTech’s vaccine manufacturing plant in Kigali.

According to Nduhungirehe, vaccines produced at the facility will benefit several African countries, including the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which continues to face multiple epidemic threats.

excerpt: Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye is scheduled to make a working visit to Rwanda on October 17, 2025, following an invitation from President Paul Kagame, according to an official statement.
title_en: Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye to Visit Rwanda
excerpt_en: Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye is scheduled to make a working visit to Rwanda on October 17, 2025, following an invitation from President Paul Kagame, according to an official statement.
body_en:
Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye is scheduled to make a working visit to Rwanda on October 17, 2025, following an invitation from President Paul Kagame, according to an official statement. The visit was approved during a Cabinet meeting in Senegal on Thursday.

The trip underscores ongoing efforts by both nations to strengthen bilateral ties. President Kagame previously became the first Rwandan head of state to visit Senegal in May 2024, shortly after assuming office, and has made multiple visits since. His most recent visit to Senegal was from August 31 to September 1, 2025, for the African Food Summit.

After Rwanda, President Faye is expected to travel to Kenya from October 19 to 21, 2025, as part of his regional engagement tour.

title: Tshisekedi Says War Spending Diverts Funds from Development
excerpt: Brussels, Belgium - Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) President Félix Antoine Tshisekedi has admitted that significant national resources that could have been directed toward public welfare, infrastructure, and…
title_en: Tshisekedi Says War Spending Diverts Funds from Development
excerpt_en: Brussels, Belgium - Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) President Félix Antoine Tshisekedi has admitted that significant national resources that could have been directed toward public welfare, infrastructure, and…
body_en:
Brussels, Belgium - Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) President Félix Antoine Tshisekedi has admitted that significant national resources that could have been directed toward public welfare, infrastructure, and agriculture have instead been diverted to sustain the ongoing war against the AFC/M23 coalition in the country’s east.

Speaking to members of the Congolese diaspora in Belgium on the sidelines of the EU-Africa Global Gateway Forum, President Tshisekedi said the conflict has drained public finances and slowed national development.

“We want peace. Because I can tell you this war is demanding a lot from us. We are refraining from giving our people many things because we have to strengthen the military and security forces,” he said, emphasizing that funds earmarked for social programs and infrastructure are being redirected to the army.

The President added that if peace could be achieved, he would gladly channel defense spending toward improving citizens’ lives. However, he insisted that he would only engage in talks with those who first condemn Rwanda, which he again accused of backing the M23 rebels - an allegation Rwanda denies.

According to reports cited by Africa Intelligence, Congo’s defense budget has surged from $459 million in 2021 to $1 billion in 2023, with a similar figure projected for 2024. From January to April 2025 alone, military expenditures reached $1 billion, driven by salary hikes for soldiers and the acquisition of new weapons systems, including tanks, Sukhoi-25 fighter jets, and Chinese-made CH-4 drones.

Sources close to the M23 claim that some of these weapons, seized during clashes in Goma, were initially intended for operations against Rwanda.

Diplomatic observers note that Tshisekedi’s approach to peace talks - both the U.S.-led mediation with Rwanda and the Qatar-facilitated negotiations with M23 - has been marked by reversals, undermining progress toward a ceasefire. Rebel leaders have repeatedly accused Kinshasa of violating truce agreements and continuing military operations.

The President’s government has also come under criticism for allegedly spending heavily on foreign lobbying campaigns to seek sanctions against Rwanda, as well as disengaging from regional economic frameworks, including the Regional Economic Integration Fund (REIF) approved by Congolese delegates in Washington on October 3, 2025.

title: Senator Evode: Tshisekedi ‘doesn’t want talks’ - only silencing will stop him, senator says
excerpt: Kigali, 12 October 2025 - Senator Uwizeyimana Evode has accused Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) President Félix Antoine Tshisekedi of acting in bad faith on peace negotiations with the AFC/M23 rebel coalition, saying…
title_en: Senator Evode: Tshisekedi ‘doesn’t want talks’ - only silencing will stop him, senator says
excerpt_en: Kigali, 12 October 2025 - Senator Uwizeyimana Evode has accused Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) President Félix Antoine Tshisekedi of acting in bad faith on peace negotiations with the AFC/M23 rebel coalition, saying…
body_en:
Kigali, 12 October 2025 - Senator Uwizeyimana Evode has accused Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) President Félix Antoine Tshisekedi of acting in bad faith on peace negotiations with the AFC/M23 rebel coalition, saying Tshisekedi gives every sign that he does not genuinely want dialogue and suggesting only force would make him stop. The senator made the remarks in an interview broadcast on Rwanda Television on the evening of Sunday, October 12, 2025.

Evode, a Rwandan senator, argued that Tshisekedi’s speeches at the EU-Africa Global Gateway Forum in Brussels and his address to the Congolese diaspora in Belgium demonstrate a public posture of peacemaking that, in Evode’s view, masks a refusal to implement key elements of negotiated settlements. “What he told Europeans - that he wants peace and reconciliation with Rwanda - is mere theater,” Evode said, adding that Tshisekedi’s words are intended to portray himself as not being the source of the problem.

Pointing to the Doha talks (Qatar-facilitated) and the Washington agreement (the U.S.-brokered package of commitments between Kinshasa and Kigali), Evode said Tshisekedi has repeatedly set red lines - notably his prior claim that he would never negotiate with the M23 - but has since reversed course in ways that, Evode contends, reveal a lack of sincerity. “During Doha he said he would never talk to M23; today there are talks, but it would not surprise us if there is no real will to implement them,” he said.

Evode framed the Doha and Washington accords as interlinked: the Doha process, he said, cannot be implemented successfully without full adherence to the Washington agreement. He accused Tshisekedi of selectively refusing provisions of the Washington deal and of obstructing measures that would neutralize armed groups and secure lasting peace in eastern DRC. “Implementing the Washington agreement would be as difficult as implementing Doha, because he has already begun rejecting parts of it,” the senator said.

In stark terms, Evode suggested Tshisekedi’s belligerent rhetoric could only be ended if the AFC/M23 acted to silence him. “He has a provocative attitude. I do not know what the AFC/M23 plan is, but he needs them to listen to him and shut him up because I see that as something that can be done,” Evode told Rwanda Television - a comment likely to inflame tensions and draw sharp criticism from Kinshasa.

Analysts say such statements reflect the deep mistrust between political actors in Kigali and Kinshasa as well as the fraught domestic politics surrounding the conflict. Whether inflammatory public comments by foreign officials or opposition figures help or hinder Doha- and Washington-led diplomacy is hotly contested; critics argue they undercut mediation and harden positions on both sides.

title: DR Congo and AFC/M23 Agree to Form Joint Ceasefire Monitoring Body
excerpt: Doha, Qatar, October 14, 2025-The Government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and the AFC/M23 coalition have reached an agreement to create a joint body responsible for overseeing the implementation of the…
title_en: DR Congo and AFC/M23 Agree to Form Joint Ceasefire Monitoring Body
excerpt_en: Doha, Qatar, October 14, 2025-The Government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and the AFC/M23 coalition have reached an agreement to create a joint body responsible for overseeing the implementation of the…
body_en:
Doha, Qatar, October 14, 2025-The Government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and the AFC/M23 coalition have reached an agreement to create a joint body responsible for overseeing the implementation of the ceasefire in North Kivu and South Kivu provinces.

This development marks the outcome of the sixth round of peace talks between both sides, held in Doha, Qatar, from October 13 to 14, 2025, under the mediation of international partners. The new mechanism is designed to strengthen transparency, rebuild trust, and prevent further violations of the fragile truce in eastern DRC.

According to the joint communiqué, the monitoring body will include:

Equal representation from the DRC government and the AFC/M23;

Observers from the African Union (AU), the State of Qatar, the United States of America, and the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR).

The committee will have the mandate to review, investigate, and document alleged ceasefire violations, and to issue weekly reports on the status of the truce and progress toward peace implementation. The first meeting of the body is expected to take place within seven days of its formation to outline its operational procedures and next steps.

The establishment of this joint mechanism follows months of disagreements over who should oversee the ceasefire. Earlier proposals to have MONUSCO, the UN peacekeeping mission in the DRC, play that role were rejected by the AFC/M23, which accused the mission of bias due to its past collaboration with the Congolese army in combat operations.

Speaking after the agreement, AFC/M23 spokesperson Lawrence Kanyuka expressed optimism, saying:

“The government of Kinshasa has signed an agreement establishing a body to monitor the ceasefire. This is a major step. We hope that this agreement will stop the repeated attacks by the Kinshasa military coalition on the civilian population.”

The latest breakthrough builds on the “Doha Principles” signed on July 19, 2025, which outlined the foundations for a broader peace agreement. While both parties had agreed to a complete cessation of hostilities, recurring clashes and mutual accusations of violations have continued to undermine trust.

Observers believe that this new step could revive momentum for peace if both sides demonstrate genuine commitment to implementing previous accords, particularly those linked to power-sharing arrangements, disarmament, and the return of displaced civilians.

The Doha process, supported by Qatar and the United States, remains one of the most significant diplomatic efforts to resolve the decade-long instability in the Great Lakes region, where overlapping security, ethnic, and political crises have persisted despite multiple peace initiatives.

title: Joseph Kabila Leads Opposition Meeting in Nairobi to Challenge Tshisekedi’s Leadership
excerpt: Nairobi, Kenya, October 14, 2025-Former President of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Joseph Kabila Kabange, has convened and is chairing a high-level meeting of opposition figures opposed to President Félix…
title_en: Joseph Kabila Leads Opposition Meeting in Nairobi to Challenge Tshisekedi’s Leadership
excerpt_en: Nairobi, Kenya, October 14, 2025-Former President of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Joseph Kabila Kabange, has convened and is chairing a high-level meeting of opposition figures opposed to President Félix…
body_en:
Nairobi, Kenya, October 14, 2025-Former President of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Joseph Kabila Kabange, has convened and is chairing a high-level meeting of opposition figures opposed to President Félix Antoine Tshisekedi. The gathering, currently taking place in Nairobi, has drawn several prominent Congolese political figures who once held senior government positions under Kabila’s administration.

Among those in attendance are Augustin Matata Ponyo, former Prime Minister (2012-2016); Seth Kikuni, a 2018 presidential candidate; Franck Diongo, leader of the MLP party; Néhémie Mwilanya, Kabila’s former chief of staff; Raymond Tshibanda, ex-Minister of Foreign Affairs; José Makila, former Deputy Prime Minister; Richard Muyej, ex-Governor of Lualaba; Kikaya Bin Karubi, former presidential advisor; and Patient Sayiba, former Director-General of OGEFREM.

Several key opposition figures were also invited but declined to attend, including Moïse Katumbi, leader of Ensemble pour la République; Martin Fayulu, who has recently pledged to support Tshisekedi in his fight against the AFC/M23 rebellion; Jean-Marc Kabund, former vice-president of the National Assembly; and Delly Sesanga, leader of Envol.

Although the meeting’s official agenda was not made public, sources close to the organizers indicate that the discussions focus on building a unified opposition coalition aimed at “rescuing the country” from what they describe as economic collapse, worsening insecurity, and social instability under Tshisekedi’s leadership.

title: Six Rwandan Senators Conclude Their Five-Year Terms
excerpt: Kigali, Rwanda, October 14, 2025-Six members of Rwanda’s Senate are preparing to complete their five-year terms in office next week, marking the end of their mandate that began in 2020.
title_en: Six Rwandan Senators Conclude Their Five-Year Terms
excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda, October 14, 2025-Six members of Rwanda’s Senate are preparing to complete their five-year terms in office next week, marking the end of their mandate that began in 2020.
body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda, October 14, 2025-Six members of Rwanda’s Senate are preparing to complete their five-year terms in office next week, marking the end of their mandate that began in 2020. Those concluding their service include Senators Evode Uwizeyimana, André Twahirwa, Clotilde Mukakarangwa, Epiphanie Kanziza, Alexis Mugisha, and Jean-Pierre Dusingizemungu.

All six were sworn in before President Paul Kagame on October 22, 2020, meaning their constitutional term officially ends on October 22, 2025.

Four were appointed by President Paul Kagame:

Evode Uwizeyimana, known for his active participation in political and legal debates.

Jean-Pierre Dusingizemungu, a historian and advocate for genocide remembrance.

Epiphanie Kanziza, a senior educator and administrator.

André Twahirwa, a long-serving public servant.

Two were elected through the Forum of Recognized Political Parties in Rwanda (NFPO):

Alexis Mugisha, representing the Democratic Green Party of Rwanda (DGPR).

Clotilde Mukakarangwa, representing the Democratic Party for the Unity of Rwanda (PDC).

Their departure opens the way for either reappointment or replacement, depending on the decisions of the President and the outcomes of internal political processes within the NFPO.

According to Article 80 of the Constitution of the Republic of Rwanda, the Senate consists of 26 members selected through different mechanisms designed to ensure political balance and institutional representation.The composition is as follows:

12 Senators are elected in accordance with the Constitution.

8 Senators are appointed by the President of the Republic.

4 Senators are elected by the Forum of Recognized Political Parties.

2 Senators are elected by higher education institutions, both public and private.

Each Senator, whether elected or appointed, serves a five-year term, which can be renewed once. The only exception applies to a former Head of State, who may serve as a Senator for life without term limits.

The rotation system of appointments and elections ensures continuity within the Senate’s operations. Of the eight Presidential appointees, four are appointed at the start of a new Senate term, while the remaining four are appointed one year later, maintaining institutional balance.

Similarly, among the four Senators elected by political parties, two are chosen at the beginning of the term, and two others a year later.

The elections for the fourth term of the Senate took place in September 2024, as part of Rwanda’s continuing effort to strengthen its legislative institutions and uphold democratic governance.

As the six Senators prepare to conclude their service, discussions are already underway regarding potential reappointments and replacements. Some of the outgoing members, particularly those appointed by the President, remain eligible for a second term if reselected.

Political analysts in Kigali note that this transition provides an opportunity for renewed perspectives within the Senate, while maintaining the institution’s balance between experience, political diversity, and technocratic expertise - a hallmark of Rwanda’s legislative system.

title: Ambassador Ngoga Urges UN to Respect Rwanda-DRC Peace Framework
excerpt: New York, October 13, 2025 - Rwanda’s Ambassador to the United Nations, Martin Ngoga, has called on UN Security Council member states to refrain from interfering in the ongoing peace process between Rwanda and the…
title_en: Ambassador Ngoga Urges UN to Respect Rwanda-DRC Peace Framework
excerpt_en: New York, October 13, 2025 - Rwanda’s Ambassador to the United Nations, Martin Ngoga, has called on UN Security Council member states to refrain from interfering in the ongoing peace process between Rwanda and the…
body_en:
New York, October 13, 2025 - Rwanda’s Ambassador to the United Nations, Martin Ngoga, has called on UN Security Council member states to refrain from interfering in the ongoing peace process between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), emphasizing that the two nations have already defined a cooperative framework to end years of conflict.

Speaking during a UN Security Council session on the security situation in the African Great Lakes Region, Ambassador Ngoga expressed concern that some member states appear to have limited or inaccurate information about the progress being made under the Washington Agreement, a bilateral peace accord signed in June 2025 with the support of the United States.

Ngoga stressed that external interference risks undermining regional peace efforts, particularly when based on misinformation or political bias. He specifically requested that the U.S. Ambassador to the UN brief the Security Council on the steps already taken under the Washington Agreement, to ensure that all nations share a factual and coordinated understanding of developments.

“The Republic of Rwanda and the DRC have agreed on how to resolve our differences,” Ngoga said.“We ask this Council to support this process. Rwanda will honor its commitments through the Washington Accords and will continue to support the Doha process.”

The Doha process, facilitated by the State of Qatar, runs parallel to the Washington Agreement and focuses on consolidating ceasefire arrangements and political dialogue between the DRC government and the AFC/M23 coalition.

Ambassador Ngoga commended Qatar and the African Union (AU) for their constructive roles in promoting dialogue and stability in the Great Lakes region. However, he warned that international involvement should be supportive, not substitutive, of African-led peace mechanisms.

“We want the contribution of this Council,” he told members.“But we also want you to give us the opportunity to fully respect these agreements - and to avoid behaving in a way that would complicate or undermine the process. What is needed is reconciliation.”

Ngoga’s remarks reflect Rwanda’s consistent stance that peace must be owned and driven by regional stakeholders, with the UN’s role focused on support and coordination, not direct intervention.

The Washington Accords, signed on June 27, 2025, outline a comprehensive framework to restore security, cooperation, and trust between Rwanda and the DRC after years of mutual accusations and armed confrontations.Its main provisions include:

Elimination of the FDLR - Both countries commit to neutralizing the FDLR (Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda), a militia that Rwanda classifies as a terrorist organization responsible for cross-border attacks.

Dismantling Rwanda’s defensive security measures - Rwanda will gradually reduce its border defense deployments once the FDLR is disbanded and the DRC ensures that no hostile forces operate from its territory.

title: AFC/M23-DRC Prisoner Release Deal Stalls Despite Qatar Talks
excerpt: The government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the AFC/M23 rebel coalition have yet to agree on the release of prisoners, despite signing a framework document on September 15, 2025, committing to the…
title_en: AFC/M23-DRC Prisoner Release Deal Stalls Despite Qatar Talks
excerpt_en: The government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the AFC/M23 rebel coalition have yet to agree on the release of prisoners, despite signing a framework document on September 15, 2025, committing to the…
body_en:
The government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the AFC/M23 rebel coalition have yet to agree on the release of prisoners, despite signing a framework document on September 15, 2025, committing to the process.

Under the agreement, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) was tasked with identifying detainees, verifying their status and facilitating their transfer between the two parties. However, one month later, no prisoners have been released, and both sides continue to accuse each other of violating the ceasefire in North Kivu and South Kivu provinces.

Talks resumed on October 13, 2025, in Qatar, where delegations from both sides met to review the implementation of the ceasefire and discuss the prisoner exchange before moving toward a broader peace agreement.

A joint monitoring mechanism was established on October 14 to oversee the ceasefire, made up of representatives from both parties, a mediator and international observers. But the prisoner issue remains unresolved.

According to sources close to the mediation, key obstacles include:

Without resolving these legal and logistical gaps, the transfer of prisoners cannot proceed, negotiators say.

The mediation team-which includes observers from the United States and the African Union-has urged both sides to accelerate progress. The peace roadmap initially aimed for a final agreement by August 2025, but the deadline has already been missed.

Talks aimed at removing the barriers to the prisoner exchange are expected to continue for up to 10 days.

The AFC/M23 has already submitted a list of detainees it wants released by the Congolese government. The list includes fighters and political allies, among them Eric Nkuba Shebandu, a former adviser to Corneille Nangaa, leader of the Congo River Alliance, who is aligned with AFC/M23.

Despite diplomatic efforts, the stalled prisoner release remains a major stumbling block in the peace process, raising fears that delays could escalate tensions on the battlefield.

title: Rwanda Inaugurates 151 km of New Roads Worth Rwf 200 Billion to Boost Trade and Connectivity
excerpt: Gicumbi, October 9, 2025 -Rwanda has officially inaugurated three newly completed asphalt roads spanning 151 kilometers, in a major infrastructure milestone aimed at enhancing trade, transport, and economic development…
title_en: Rwanda Inaugurates 151 km of New Roads Worth Rwf 200 Billion to Boost Trade and Connectivity
excerpt_en: Gicumbi, October 9, 2025 -Rwanda has officially inaugurated three newly completed asphalt roads spanning 151 kilometers, in a major infrastructure milestone aimed at enhancing trade, transport, and economic development…
body_en:
Gicumbi, October 9, 2025 -Rwanda has officially inaugurated three newly completed asphalt roads spanning 151 kilometers, in a major infrastructure milestone aimed at enhancing trade, transport, and economic development across several districts. The projects, valued at over Rwf 200 billion, were launched during a ceremony held in Rukomo Sector, Gicumbi District.

The projects were financed through partnerships between the Government of Rwanda and several Arab development institutions, including the Arab Bank for Economic Development in Africa (BADEA), the Saudi Fund for Development (SFD), the Kuwait Fund for Arab Economic Development (KFAED), and the OPEC Fund for International Development (OFID).

- Infrastructure Driving Growth

Speaking at the ceremony, Jean de Dieu Uwihanganye, Secretary of State in the Ministry of Infrastructure, said the new roads are already spurring growth in agriculture, trade, and livestock sectors.

“These roads have been in use for some time, but their official completion marks a turning point for regional development,” Uwihanganye said. “Infrastructure plays a key role in improving the economy and the livelihoods of people living along these routes.”

He also announced plans to install street lighting on the Nyagatare-Rukomo road, adding that the projects’ surplus budget had already funded lighting works along the 23-kilometer Rubengera-Gisiza section.

- Trade and Connectivity Benefits

Gasana Stephen, Mayor of Nyagatare District, highlighted the Rukomo-Nyagatare road as a “pillar of trade facilitation,” reducing travel time between Kigali and the northeastern regions.

“The road has transformed business connectivity in our area. Farmers and traders can now move their goods faster and more safely,” he said.

- International Partners Commend Rwanda’s Vision

Fahad Abdullah Aldossari, President of BADEA, reaffirmed the bank’s commitment to supporting Rwanda’s transport sector, noting that out of $300 million in total funding to the country, $132 million has gone directly into road construction.

“We believe that investing in roads accelerates growth and connects communities,” Aldossari stated.

- Boost for Tourism and Regional Integration

Northern Province Governor Mugabowagahunde Maurice said the new roads will serve as “a backbone for tourism and commerce,” particularly in linking major agricultural and touristic hubs.

“Our administration is committed to building complementary infrastructure so that residents and businesses can fully benefit from these investments,” he said.

The inauguration underscores Rwanda’s broader push to modernize its transport network, improve regional integration, and facilitate cross-border trade - key pillars of the National Strategy for Transformation (NST1) and Vision 2050.

title: Western Province: 15 Tons of Sambaza Caught in One Night as Lake Kivu Reopens After Two-Month Fishing Ban
excerpt: Fishermen operating on Lake Kivu are celebrating a record haul after catching more than 15 tons of sambaza (small sardine fish) on the first night following the end of a two-month fishing ban.
title_en: Western Province: 15 Tons of Sambaza Caught in One Night as Lake Kivu Reopens After Two-Month Fishing Ban
excerpt_en: Fishermen operating on Lake Kivu are celebrating a record haul after catching more than 15 tons of sambaza (small sardine fish) on the first night following the end of a two-month fishing ban.
body_en:
Fishermen operating on Lake Kivu are celebrating a record haul after catching more than 15 tons of sambaza (small sardine fish) on the first night following the end of a two-month fishing ban. The surge in catches has sparked optimism among local cooperatives and district officials across Rwanda’s Western Province.

The temporary closure, known as the “fishermen’s holiday,” was instituted by the Ministry of Agriculture and Animal Resources (MINAGRI) at the request of local fishing cooperatives. The measure, which ran from August 9 to October 9, 2025, was aimed at allowing fish stocks to regenerate after months of sharp decline in yields observed between June and July.

4.5 tons in Nyamasheke,

5 tons in Rutsiro,

1.7 tons in Karongi,

2 tons in Rubavu, and

2.3 tons in Rusizi.

Overall sambaza production nearly doubled compared to the same reopening period last year, rising from 7 tons to 15 tons.

Fishermen credit tighter controls and anti-poaching efforts

The head of the Karongi District Fishermen’s Association, Ndagijimana Emmanuel, attributed the increase to coordinated efforts between fishermen, local authorities, and security agencies to combat illegal fishing during the closure.

“We have arrested several poachers who continued fishing when the lake was closed,” he said. “Previously, a kilo of sambaza sold for between 6,000 and 7,000 francs, but now with increased supply, prices are stabilizing.”

He added that production per boat had also risen dramatically:

“Before the closure, a group of three boats using 35,000 francs worth of fuel could barely catch three to five kilos. Now, a successful fisherman can catch up to 80 kilos, while others bring in at least 15 kilos. The current market price is around 3,350 francs per kilo.”

A long journey for sambaza in Rwanda

Sibomana Jean Bosco, head of the Karongi branch of the national fisheries project, hailed the progress in Rwanda’s fishing industry, recalling that sambaza were first introduced into Lake Kivu in 1959 from Lake Tanganyika, with commercial fishing beginning in 1978.

“At that time, many Rwandans didn’t eat sambaza - people believed it was harmful to cows and milk,” he explained. “Fishermen used to throw sambaza back into the lake because there were no buyers. Today, the situation is completely different: the market demand is strong, and people understand the nutritional value of fish products.”

While celebrating the bumper catch, Kwitonda Théoneste, chairperson of the Karongi District Commission for Monitoring Fish Quality and Pricing, warned that illegal fishing remains a challenge.

“Although we’ve made good progress against poaching, some illegal fishers still sneaked onto the lake during the closure period,” he said.

Officials say continued collaboration between cooperatives, local government, and law enforcement will be key to maintaining sustainable fishing practices and protecting the lake’s ecosystem.

title: Rwanda Needs $12 Billion to Cut Greenhouse Gas Emissions by 2035
excerpt: The Rwanda Environment Management Authority (REMA) has announced that the country will require over $12 billion in funding to achieve its target of reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 53% by 2035, as part of its…
title_en: Rwanda Needs $12 Billion to Cut Greenhouse Gas Emissions by 2035
excerpt_en: The Rwanda Environment Management Authority (REMA) has announced that the country will require over $12 billion in funding to achieve its target of reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 53% by 2035, as part of its…
body_en:
The Rwanda Environment Management Authority (REMA) has announced that the country will require over $12 billion in funding to achieve its target of reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 53% by 2035, as part of its long-term climate resilience strategy.

According to REMA, the investment will support nationwide efforts to transition toward a low-carbon and climate-resilient economy, with key funding directed toward renewable energy, sustainable agriculture, green infrastructure, and industrial efficiency.

A substantial share of the funds will go to clean energy projects, including the expansion of solar power and other renewable sources. Rwanda also plans to promote electric mobility, reduce dependence on fossil fuels such as wood and coal, and scale up the use of biogas and methane gas generation.

Officials estimate that these measures could cut up to 6.24 million tonnes (Mt) of greenhouse gas emissions.

Beyond energy, part of the investment will focus on enhancing energy efficiency in both industrial and household activities to make clean energy affordable and sustainable across the country.

The initiative aligns with Rwanda’s Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) under the Paris Agreement, reaffirming its commitment to environmental protection and a green economy.

title: Rwanda Honored as Partner Country at Poland’s TT Warsaw 2025 Trade Fair
excerpt: Rwanda has been awarded a prestigious honor for excellence and innovation, being named the Partner Country of the TT Warsaw 2025 International Travel and Tourism Fair, one of Europe’s most established trade events held…
title_en: Rwanda Honored as Partner Country at Poland’s TT Warsaw 2025 Trade Fair
excerpt_en: Rwanda has been awarded a prestigious honor for excellence and innovation, being named the Partner Country of the TT Warsaw 2025 International Travel and Tourism Fair, one of Europe’s most established trade events held…
body_en:
Rwanda has been awarded a prestigious honor for excellence and innovation, being named the Partner Country of the TT Warsaw 2025 International Travel and Tourism Fair, one of Europe’s most established trade events held annually in the Polish capital, Warsaw.

This marks Rwanda’s first participation in the fair’s 30-year history, where the Rwanda Development Board (RDB) was given the opportunity to showcase the country’s growing tourism industry during the official opening ceremony, attended by Poland’s Minister of Tourism and Sports.

Rwanda’s delegation was led by Ambassador Prof. Anastase Shyaka, who, in his keynote remarks, highlighted the strong bilateral ties between Rwanda and Poland, and expressed gratitude to the organizers for selecting Rwanda as the fair’s partner of honor.

“It is a sign of Rwanda’s diversity, and Rwanda is a great host,” Amb. Shyaka said, encouraging visitors to explore the country’s tourism offerings.

The Polish Minister of Tourism and Sports praised Rwanda’s organizational excellence, noting its successful preparations to host the 2025 UCI Road World Championships in Kigali.

Rwanda’s booth featured eight tourism and hospitality companies, showcasing the country’s natural beauty, cultural heritage, and investment opportunities in the travel sector. The event also included a performance by the Icyeza Polish troupe, who presented the traditional Rwandan cow dance, to the delight of the audience.

title: Rwanda Calls on Investors to Boost Renewable Energy and Circular Economy Initiatives
excerpt: The Director of Trade and Investment at the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MINICOM), Doreen Ntawebasa, has urged both local and international investors to seize the growing opportunities in Rwanda’s renewable energy…
title_en: Rwanda Calls on Investors to Boost Renewable Energy and Circular Economy Initiatives
excerpt_en: The Director of Trade and Investment at the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MINICOM), Doreen Ntawebasa, has urged both local and international investors to seize the growing opportunities in Rwanda’s renewable energy…
body_en:
The Director of Trade and Investment at the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MINICOM), Doreen Ntawebasa, has urged both local and international investors to seize the growing opportunities in Rwanda’s renewable energy sector, describing it as one of the country’s most promising frontiers for sustainable development and modern agriculture.

Speaking at a high-level meeting on October 1, 2025, which brought together members of the private sector, renewable energy companies, investors, and government agencies, Ntawebasa highlighted the need for bold investments that will help green innovations reach large-scale impact.

“Rwanda’s goal is to develop the economy using what we have,” she said. “We must transform available resources - from land to by-products - into valuable goods, whether for agriculture, animal feed, or energy production.”

Ntawebasa emphasized that many Rwandan companies are already developing environmentally friendly technologies despite limited funding, and called for stronger partnerships to scale up their operations.

One of the success stories shared at the event came from Kigasali Coffee Company Ltd, whose representative Niyigena Consolée explained how coffee husks from the company’s processing plant are being converted into eco-friendly charcoal briquettes.

“Our charcoal emits fewer greenhouse gases and reduces the need for wood-based charcoal,” Niyigena said. “We currently produce 300 kilograms a day, but with new machinery and more investment, we could produce several tons daily - creating more jobs and protecting the environment.”

The discussion also highlighted Rwanda’s growing circular economy sector, which focuses on recycling waste - especially food waste - into new agricultural and industrial products. The initiative began in 2023 under the ‘Circular Food System for Rwanda’ project, managed by the National Industrial Research and Development Agency (NIRDA) and supported by the World Bank.

Eric Ruzigamanzi, the World Bank’s project director for the initiative, said the goal is to link innovative enterprises with investors who can help them scale up.

“These companies have the potential to create jobs, strengthen the economy, and promote environmental sustainability,” Ruzigamanzi said. “But to achieve that, they need capital - and that’s why we’re building bridges between them and investors.”

The conference brought together 20 companies operating in renewable energy and circular economy sectors, each presenting innovative projects designed to reduce waste, boost clean energy production, and promote Rwanda’s green industrial transformation.

The initiative began in 2023 under the ‘Circular Food System for Rwanda’ project, managed by the National Industrial Research and Development Agency (NIRDA) and supported by the World Bank.

Eric Ruzigamanzi, the World Bank’s project director for the initiative, said the goal is to link innovative enterprises with investors who can help them scale up.

“These companies have the potential to create jobs, strengthen the economy, and promote environmental sustainability,” Ruzigamanzi said. “But to achieve that, they need capital - and that’s why we’re building bridges between them and investors.”

The conference brought together 20 companies operating in renewable energy and circular economy sectors, each presenting innovative projects designed to reduce waste, boost clean energy production, and promote Rwanda’s green industrial transformation.

title: Minister Gasore Outlines Future Use of Kigali and Bugesera Airports
excerpt: Dr. Jimmy Gasore, Rwanda’s Minister of Infrastructure, has provided details on the future roles of Kigali International Airport (Kanombe) and the new Bugesera International Airport once construction is completed.
title_en: Minister Gasore Outlines Future Use of Kigali and Bugesera Airports
excerpt_en: Dr. Jimmy Gasore, Rwanda’s Minister of Infrastructure, has provided details on the future roles of Kigali International Airport (Kanombe) and the new Bugesera International Airport once construction is completed.
body_en:
Dr. Jimmy Gasore, Rwanda’s Minister of Infrastructure, has provided details on the future roles of Kigali International Airport (Kanombe) and the new Bugesera International Airport once construction is completed. Speaking on October 9, 2025, after meeting with Senators on the Committee on Foreign Affairs, Cooperation, and Security, Gasore confirmed that Kanombe Airport will no longer handle large passenger or cargo aircraft once the Bugesera facility becomes operational.

“Large passenger and cargo aircraft will not continue to use Kigali Airport in Kanombe. We will explore other activities to keep the airport productive,” he said.

Construction of Bugesera International Airport is progressing steadily, with completion expected by 2027 and full operation targeted for mid-2028. The project covers an area of approximately 900 hectares.

To ensure efficient connectivity, Gasore announced plans for three major roads linking the new airport to Kigali and surrounding areas, with construction scheduled to begin in early 2026.

“The roads will connect Masaka to the airport, the back part of Bugesera, and the Kicukiro bridge to the airport. Studies have been completed, and tenders will be issued soon,” he added.

The new infrastructure is designed to improve travel and cargo handling, positioning Bugesera International Airport as Rwanda’s primary hub for international flights, while Kanombe will focus on alternative aviation-related activities.

title: RSB Certifies 1,000 SMEs Under ‘Zamukana Ubusunga’ Program
excerpt: Kigali, Rwanda - The Rwanda Standards Board (RSB) has announced that 1,000 small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) have been certified under its ‘Zamukana Ubusunga’ program, which was launched in 2017 to help local…
title_en: RSB Certifies 1,000 SMEs Under ‘Zamukana Ubusunga’ Program
excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda - The Rwanda Standards Board (RSB) has announced that 1,000 small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) have been certified under its ‘Zamukana Ubusunga’ program, which was launched in 2017 to help local…
body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda - The Rwanda Standards Board (RSB) has announced that 1,000 small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) have been certified under its ‘Zamukana Ubusunga’ program, which was launched in 2017 to help local businesses meet quality standards and compete internationally.

The initiative focuses on supporting youth-, women-, and disability-led enterprises that face barriers in meeting production and quality requirements. By improving product standards, the program aims to reduce imports and strengthen Rwanda’s manufacturing base.

According to Jerome Ndahimana, Director of Zamukana Ubutenge at RSB, awareness and participation have grown significantly since the program’s inception. In 2024 alone, over 250 enterprises joined the scheme.

During the World Standards Organization’s annual meeting, Rwanda showcased Zamukana Ubusunga as an effective model for SME quality promotion.

The progress aligns with Rwanda’s broader industrial growth: according to the National Institute of Statistics of Rwanda (NISR), the industrial sector grew by 8.3% in August 2025 compared to the same period in 2024. Rwanda’s GDP reached Rwf18,785 billion in 2024, up from Rwf16,626 billion the previous year, with services contributing 48% and agriculture 25%.

title: IHS Sells Rwanda Tower Operations to Paradigm Tower Ventures for $274.5 Million
excerpt: Kigali, Rwanda ,October 2025-IHS Holding Limited, one of the world’s largest owners and operators of telecommunications tower infrastructure, has sold 100% of its Rwandan operations to Paradigm Tower Ventures in a deal…
title_en: IHS Sells Rwanda Tower Operations to Paradigm Tower Ventures for $274.5 Million
excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda ,October 2025-IHS Holding Limited, one of the world’s largest owners and operators of telecommunications tower infrastructure, has sold 100% of its Rwandan operations to Paradigm Tower Ventures in a deal…
body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda ,October 2025-IHS Holding Limited, one of the world’s largest owners and operators of telecommunications tower infrastructure, has sold 100% of its Rwandan operations to Paradigm Tower Ventures in a deal valued at $274.5 million, marking a major shift in Rwanda’s telecommunications infrastructure market.

The transaction, which covers 1,456 towers currently owned by IHS Rwanda, is pending final approval by relevant regulatory authorities and is expected to be completed in the coming days.

According to a statement from IHS Towers’ management, the sale aligns with the company’s broader strategy to optimize its portfolio and enhance shareholder value, focusing on higher-growth markets and asset efficiency. IHS had first announced its intention to divest its Rwandan operations in May 2025, and the completion of the sale marks its full exit from the country.

With this acquisition, Paradigm Tower Ventures becomes the first independent tower investment company in sub-Saharan Africa, positioning itself as a major player in the region’s rapidly expanding digital infrastructure sector.

Backed by prominent financial institutions - including Convergence Partners and Rand Merchant Bank (RMB), a division of FirstRand Bank Limited - Paradigm aims to accelerate the modernization of Rwanda’s telecom infrastructure and expand network capacity.

Stephen Harris, CEO and co-founder of Paradigm, expressed optimism about the acquisition and Rwanda’s investment climate:

“Rwanda is an exciting market, where there is a huge need for infrastructure. Paradigm’s team is ready to build an investment based on providing quality services, and constructing reliable infrastructure for telecommunications companies.”

IHS Holding began its Rwandan operations in 2013, when it acquired MTN Rwandacell Ltd’s tower assets and later took over Rwanda Towers Ltd, a former subsidiary of Airtel Rwanda Ltd. Over the past decade, IHS Rwanda has played a key role in strengthening the country’s mobile coverage and supporting its ICT-driven Vision 2050 strategy.

Industry analysts view this transaction as a significant milestone for both companies - signaling IHS’s ongoing portfolio rationalization across Africa, and Paradigm’s emergence as a regional infrastructure consolidator. The sale also reflects the growing attractiveness of Rwanda’s telecommunications market, driven by digital transformation policies, stable regulation, and rising demand for broadband and mobile services.

title: More than 80% of traders in Kigali are not registered with the Private Sector Federation (PSF).
excerpt: According to a census presented at the PSF Kigali City General Assembly held on October 17, 2025.
title_en: More than 80% of traders in Kigali are not registered with the Private Sector Federation (PSF).
excerpt_en: According to a census presented at the PSF Kigali City General Assembly held on October 17, 2025.
body_en:
According to a census presented at the PSF Kigali City General Assembly held on October 17, 2025. The survey shows that Kigali has 57,325 traders, including over 23,000 in Gasabo, 15,000 in Kicukiro and 17,000 in Nyarugenge, yet only 9,700 are PSF members - just 17.4%.

PSF Kigali General Manager Tharcisse Ngabonziza attributed the low membership to limited awareness among business operators. “This is mainly due to lack of information. We are holding meetings at sector and district levels to increase sensitization, and we will not give up,” he said.

PSF highlighted member benefits such as business advocacy, networking and access to timely information, as well as initiatives like the PSF Health Scheme and capacity-building training.

Representing Kinyinya Sector, Emmanuel Ntuyenabo welcomed the progress made: “We appreciate the achievements, especially access to health insurance. Good health is the greatest asset,” he said.

Established in 1999, PSF has operated for 26 years. Membership starts at 6,000 Rwf. Over the past three years, PSF members in Kigali have contributed 213 million Rwf, including 47 million in 2023, 132 million in 2024 and 38 million in 2025.

title: Rwandan Private Sector Says Border Incident with Burundi Sparked Local Maize Seed Production
excerpt: The Head of Advocacy at the Private Sector Federation (PSF), Callixte Kanamugire, has revealed that a 2013 border standoff with Burundi over a shipment of maize seeds pushed Rwanda to accelerate local seed production…
title_en: Rwandan Private Sector Says Border Incident with Burundi Sparked Local Maize Seed Production
excerpt_en: The Head of Advocacy at the Private Sector Federation (PSF), Callixte Kanamugire, has revealed that a 2013 border standoff with Burundi over a shipment of maize seeds pushed Rwanda to accelerate local seed production…
body_en:
The Head of Advocacy at the Private Sector Federation (PSF), Callixte Kanamugire, has revealed that a 2013 border standoff with Burundi over a shipment of maize seeds pushed Rwanda to accelerate local seed production and reduce reliance on imports.

Speaking during the PSF General Assembly held in Kigali on October 17, 2025, Kanamugire said the private sector has been instrumental in cutting Rwanda’s import dependence by investing in domestic production.

For years, Rwanda imported agricultural seeds, especially maize, from Zambia, Kenya and Tanzania due to limited local production. However, Kanamugire recalled a turning point more than a decade ago when Burundi blocked Rwandan-bound trucks carrying maize seeds from Zambia.

“Trucks came from Zambia, about 18 or 20, and reached the Burundi-Rwanda border. The Burundians refused to let them cross. That was around 2013,” Kanamugire recounted. “The maize had to be returned to Bujumbura, shipped back to Zambia and re-exported to Rwanda through Tanzania.”

The disruption delayed maize planting by up to three weeks and caused significant losses, affecting harvests and crippling maize processing factories that relied on the delayed supply.

According to Kanamugire, the incident exposed Rwanda’s vulnerability to external supply shocks and “woke up the private sector,” which began investing in seed multiplication programs to boost local production.

“Within two years, maize seeds started being produced in Rwanda,” he said. “The country needed 3,500 tonnes per quarter, and local producers were already supplying 5,000 tonnes. This shows the potential we have but are not fully using.”

Kanamugire emphasized that Rwanda must increase domestic production to cut imports and save foreign currency.

“Buying goods from abroad consumes a lot of foreign exchange. We must produce locally and export to earn forex, which can be used for essential imports like medicines and medical equipment,” he said.

Rwanda currently has 85 large-scale agro-processing industries and 608 small-scale processing plants. Despite this growth, the country still relies heavily on imports. In 2024, Rwanda imported goods worth $6.5 billion, up from $3.1 billion in 2017, leaving a trade deficit of $2.3 billion.

The government has recently prioritized agricultural transformation and industrialization to reduce its import bill. Last year, Rwanda also announced that fruits consumed locally are now being sourced from within the country, further boosting import substitution efforts.

title: Gisagara Women Save Over Rwf 140 Million Through Community Groups
excerpt: Women in Gisagara District have saved more than Rwf 143 million through small neighborhood savings groups, a model they say has transformed their economic lives and strengthened financial independence in rural…
title_en: Gisagara Women Save Over Rwf 140 Million Through Community Groups
excerpt_en: Women in Gisagara District have saved more than Rwf 143 million through small neighborhood savings groups, a model they say has transformed their economic lives and strengthened financial independence in rural…
body_en:
Women in Gisagara District have saved more than Rwf 143 million through small neighborhood savings groups, a model they say has transformed their economic lives and strengthened financial independence in rural communities.

The achievement was celebrated in Kibilizi Sector during Rwanda’s commemoration of the 28th International Day of Rural Women.

According to district figures, the savings come from 126 groups, 85% of whose members are women. Each group is made up of 25 members who contribute Rwf 500 per week, with a maximum of five shares per person, equivalent to Rwf 2,500 weekly. The groups distribute accumulated funds based on individual contributions and savings records.

Members also say the initiative has enabled them to pay Mutuelle de Santé (community-based health insurance) and invest in small businesses without difficulty-seen as one of the most immediate benefits of the saving scheme.

The groups not only save money but also engage in income-generating activities using simple digital financial services. As of October 1, 2025, one group had saved Rwf 2 million, while another had invested Rwf 6 million in trading.

One member, Mukaneza Clémentine, shared her success story. Initially a rice and cassava farmer, she said agriculture alone was not lifting her out of poverty. After joining a savings group, she took a loan of Rwf 200,000 to start trading electronically. With discipline and training from World Relief Rwanda, her capital has now grown to over Rwf 1.5 million. She has also built a family home and runs a boutique selling electronic accessories.

Another member, Bampire Béatha, from the KOABIDU Maize Cooperative, which brings together over 700 women, testified that saving culture has transformed their cooperative. They now plan to buy a transport vehicle and build commercial structures worth over Rwf 50 million.

World Relief Rwanda Says Savings Model Reduces Poverty

Yannick Niyireba, Project Manager at World Relief Rwanda, said the organization works with more than 400 savings groups, including those in Gisagara. He noted that over 80% of participants improve their livelihoods significantly through savings, while over 50% move out of extreme poverty categories.

“These groups teach financial discipline, loan management and confidence to invest. Even farmers are able to borrow and repay after harvest without falling into debt traps,” he explained.

The Deputy Mayor of Gisagara District in charge of Economic Development, Jean Paul Habineza, hailed women-led savings and credit groups as a powerful driver of development.

“Beyond helping pay for Mutuelle and Ejo Heza long-term savings, these groups support entrepreneurship and reduce financial waste. They empower women and strengthen families,” he said.

Local leaders and partners called for continued support to expand the initiative across rural communities, promoting financial literacy and economic resilience among women.
