title: Bank of Kigali Celebrates Diwali, Pledges Support to Indian Entrepreneurs in Rwanda
excerpt: The Bank of Kigali joined the Indian community in Kigali to celebrate Diwali, the festival of lights, pledging continued financial support to Indians running businesses across Rwanda.
title_en: Bank of Kigali Celebrates Diwali, Pledges Support to Indian Entrepreneurs in Rwanda
excerpt_en: The Bank of Kigali joined the Indian community in Kigali to celebrate Diwali, the festival of lights, pledging continued financial support to Indians running businesses across Rwanda.
body_en:
The Bank of Kigali joined the Indian community in Kigali to celebrate Diwali, the festival of lights, pledging continued financial support to Indians running businesses across Rwanda. The celebration took place on October 11, 2025, at MD Hill Garden in Kimironko, Gasabo District, drawing members of the Indian diaspora and showcasing the community’s cultural traditions.

Diwali, derived from the Sanskrit word Deepavali meaning “a series of lights,” is celebrated over five days, with the third day considered the main day of the festival. Traditionally, it is a time for family reunions, gift-giving, charity, and reflection, with homes decorated with clay lamps and candles.

In Kigali, the festivities included performances by popular Indian artists and musicians, such as Nitin Shankar, Anup Shankar, Mayur Datta, Deepak Walke, Brijesh Shah, Ganesh Thorat, Arif Sheikh, Rupali Ghogare, Jyoti Shankar, Sanchari Sengupta, and Ram Deshpande, with music from iconic Bollywood films delighting attendees.

Mukunzi Darius, Head of Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises at Bank of Kigali, expressed the bank’s commitment to supporting the Indian business community in Rwanda.

“We are very happy to celebrate Diwali with Indians living in Rwanda. We appreciate their important role in business, particularly in industry, healthcare, and essential goods,” he said.

Darius emphasized that the bank offers tailored financial services for all sectors, including corporates, SMEs, agribusiness, and livestock, aiming to help Indian entrepreneurs grow their businesses. “To the entire Indian community, we wish that the festival of lights illuminates your lives with happiness, peace, and success,” he added.

According to the Rwanda Development Board (RDB), Indian investors contributed $445.1 million across 35 projects in 2024, highlighting the diaspora’s significant role in Rwanda’s economic development.

The Bank of Kigali’s partnership with the Indian community reflects ongoing efforts to support cross-cultural entrepreneurship and strengthen Rwanda’s growing investment landscape.

title_en: EU Grants Rwanda €95 Million to Boost Vaccine Production and Health Innovation
excerpt_en: BRUSSELS - The European Union has pledged €95 million (approximately 130 billion Rwandan francs) to support Rwanda’s growing role in vaccine production and biomedical innovation, further cementing Kigali’s position as a…
body_en:
BRUSSELS - The European Union has pledged €95 million (approximately 130 billion Rwandan francs) to support Rwanda’s growing role in vaccine production and biomedical innovation, further cementing Kigali’s position as a leading health hub in Africa.

The announcement came following a meeting on October 9, 2025, between Rwandan President Paul Kagame and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on the sidelines of the EU-Africa Global Gateway Forum in Belgium. The discussions centered on bilateral cooperation, public health, and EU support for Rwanda’s vaccine production capacity, particularly through the BioNTech mRNA vaccine factory in Kigali.

According to a statement from the Office of the President (Urugwiro Village), the two leaders also met with European Investment Bank (EIB) President Nadia Calviño and BioNTech CEO Uğur Şahin to formalize the €95 million funding package aimed at strengthening Rwanda’s biopharmaceutical sector.

Opened in 2023, the BioNTech facility in Kigali-funded through the EU’s Global Gateway initiative-was the first of its kind in Africa. It was designed to address vaccine shortages and enhance local production capacity across the continent. President Kagame has previously emphasized that the project will reduce Africa’s dependency on imported medicines and vaccines, enabling the continent to better respond to future pandemics.

Von der Leyen, writing on X (formerly Twitter), reiterated the EU’s commitment to Rwanda’s peace and development efforts, highlighting support for the Rwanda-DRC peace process mediated by the United States.

“We support the peace agreement between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, backed by the U.S.,” von der Leyen said. “The European Union stands ready to support President Kagame’s path toward peace and sustainable investment in the region.”

She added that the new €95 million investment underscores the EU’s trust in Rwanda’s vision of becoming a continental hub for medicine and innovation, strengthening its leadership in Africa’s public health transformation.

The meeting came amid continued diplomatic friction in the region, as President Félix Tshisekedi of the DRC once again delayed cooperation efforts with Rwanda, blocking the signing of a bilateral economic partnership agreement earlier in October.

Despite these challenges, the EU’s renewed investment signals international confidence in Rwanda’s governance, stability, and scientific capacity, marking another milestone in its rise as a model for African-led innovation in global health.

title: Kamonyi: Howo Truck Accident Kills Two, Injures 11
excerpt: A serious Howo truck accident in Kamonyi District left two people dead and 11 others injured, including two in critical condition, on October 15, 2025, authorities confirmed.
title_en: Kamonyi: Howo Truck Accident Kills Two, Injures 11
excerpt_en: A serious Howo truck accident in Kamonyi District left two people dead and 11 others injured, including two in critical condition, on October 15, 2025, authorities confirmed.
body_en:
A serious Howo truck accident in Kamonyi District left two people dead and 11 others injured, including two in critical condition, on October 15, 2025, authorities confirmed.

The incident occurred around 5:00 p.m. in Ruyenzi Center, Runda Sector, when the truck, loaded with sand, was traveling along Gihara Road toward Ruyenzi. According to Southern Province Police Spokesperson, CIP Kamanzi Hassan, the vehicle collided with five other vehicles and several pedestrians. Two victims died instantly at the scene.

Two of the seriously injured were transferred to Kigali University Hospital (CHUK), while others received treatment at La Frontière, UB Caritas, and Gihara Health Center.

Police suspect a technical failure in the truck’s braking system caused the accident. The driver has been detained at Runda Police Station while authorities prepare a report to be submitted for judicial action.

CIP Kamanzi expressed condolences to the families of the deceased and wished a speedy recovery for the injured, emphasizing the police’s commitment to conducting a thorough investigation.

title: Rwandan Prisons See Gradual Decline in Overcrowding, Yet Some Facilities Remain Strained
excerpt: Rwanda’s National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) has reported that the country’s prison population has decreased, though several facilities remain overcrowded, according to its 2024/2025 activity report.
title_en: Rwandan Prisons See Gradual Decline in Overcrowding, Yet Some Facilities Remain Strained
excerpt_en: Rwanda’s National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) has reported that the country’s prison population has decreased, though several facilities remain overcrowded, according to its 2024/2025 activity report.
body_en:
Rwanda’s National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) has reported that the country’s prison population has decreased, though several facilities remain overcrowded, according to its 2024/2025 activity report.

As of August 31, 2025, 74,253 people were held in Rwanda’s 14 prisons, including 68,944 men, 4,773 women, 516 boys, and 20 girls. The overall prison overcrowding rate has dropped from 134.3% to 110%, representing a 24.3% reduction, but certain facilities continue to operate beyond capacity.

Rubavu Prison: Holds 6,214 inmates, including 1,206 convicted of genocide, with a capacity of 4,480. Overcrowding stands at 138.7%.

Rwamagana Prison: 17,046 prisoners, 2,258 convicted of genocide, capacity 13,797 (123.5% overcrowded).

Muhanga Prison: 6,544 inmates, 700 for genocide, capacity 5,250 (124.6% overcrowded).

Nyarugenge Prison (Mageragere): 10,785 inmates, 1,126 genocide convicts, capacity 8,662 (124.5% overcrowded).

Rusizi Prison: 3,069 inmates, 792 for genocide, capacity 2,500 (122.7% overcrowded).

Huye Prison: 10,146 inmates, 3,841 genocide convicts, capacity 9,700 (104.5% overcrowded).

Bugesera Prison: 2,879 inmates, 1,017 genocide convicts, capacity 2,800 (102.8% overcrowded).

Nyamagabe Prison: 1,839 inmates, 833 genocide convicts, capacity 3,035 (60.5% capacity).

Mulindi Military Prison: 610 inmates, 12 genocide convicts, capacity 800.

Musanze Prison: 4,886 inmates, 150 genocide convicts, capacity 5,887 (82.9% capacity).

Ngoma Prison: 1,286 inmates, 325 genocide convicts, capacity 1,500.

Nyanza (Mpanga) Prison: 5,233 inmates, 3,542 genocide convicts, capacity 5,500 (95% capacity).

Nyagatare Prison: 647 juvenile offenders, 63 genocide-related, capacity 650 (99.5% capacity).

NHRC Chairperson Umurungi Providence told Parliament that the Department of Corrections reported 71,561 detainees, representing 103.8% of national prison capacity as of late August 2025.

The report emphasizes that while Rwanda has made progress in reducing overcrowding, several major facilities, particularly those housing genocide convicts, continue to exceed capacity, highlighting the need for ongoing reforms in the corrections system.

title: Rwanda Reaffirms Commitment to Refugee Rights and Welfare
excerpt: Rwanda has reiterated its dedication to protecting the rights of refugees, ensuring they live in security and dignity across the country, according to the Rwanda Human Rights Commission (NHRC).
title_en: Rwanda Reaffirms Commitment to Refugee Rights and Welfare
excerpt_en: Rwanda has reiterated its dedication to protecting the rights of refugees, ensuring they live in security and dignity across the country, according to the Rwanda Human Rights Commission (NHRC).
body_en:
Rwanda has reiterated its dedication to protecting the rights of refugees, ensuring they live in security and dignity across the country, according to the Rwanda Human Rights Commission (NHRC). Chairperson Umurungi Providence highlighted these achievements while presenting the Commission’s 2024/2025 report and outlining plans for 2025/2026.

Monitoring activities covered five refugee camps, two temporary sites, and urban areas. The NHRC recorded a total of 135,952 refugees, including:

Camps: 120,618 (27,372 men, 32,989 women, 30,185 boys, 30,072 girls)

Temporary camps: 3,627 (1,138 men, 977 women, 749 boys, 763 girls)

Urban and other areas: 11,707 (5,457 men, 2,718 women, 1,842 boys, 1,690 girls)

As of October 10, 2025, Rwanda hosted 137,773 refugees, including 83,923 Congolese, 52,614 Burundians, and 1,236 from other countries.

The Commission confirmed that refugees enjoy full civil, political, economic, social, and cultural rights. They can move freely within Rwanda and, except for their country of origin, travel internationally using a refugee travel document issued by the National Immigration Agency.

Refugees and asylum seekers are provided with identification documents. Refugee identity cards, now valid for 10 years instead of five, allow holders to access services and, if they meet legal requirements, marry before a civil registry office.

Refugees are represented in courts for legal disputes or criminal accusations, with support from Prison Fellowship Rwanda. Security within camps is maintained jointly by the Rwandan Police, refugee patrols, and the Judicial Police Department.

Umurungi noted that infrastructure improvements are needed, citing the Mahama camp, where poor road conditions and limited electricity pose safety risks.

The Commission found that many refugees are economically active, engaging in agriculture, livestock, handicrafts, and small businesses. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization provides monthly assistance based on vulnerability:

Despite these efforts, some refugees in the most vulnerable categories continue to face financial difficulties. The Commission also reported isolated cases of fraud by refugees using small loans.

Rwanda ensures refugees have access to education, employment, healthcare, and other essential services, demonstrating the country’s ongoing commitment to integrating displaced populations safely and respectfully.

The NHRC plans to continue monitoring refugee rights and addressing infrastructure, safety, and livelihood challenges in the coming year.

title: UN to Cut 25% of Peacekeeping Troops Amid U.S. Funding Reductions
excerpt: NEW YORK - The United Nations has announced plans to reduce its global peacekeeping force by 25%, a move prompted by significant U.S. funding cuts under President Donald Trump’s foreign aid reduction plan.
title_en: UN to Cut 25% of Peacekeeping Troops Amid U.S. Funding Reductions
excerpt_en: NEW YORK - The United Nations has announced plans to reduce its global peacekeeping force by 25%, a move prompted by significant U.S. funding cuts under President Donald Trump’s foreign aid reduction plan.
body_en:
NEW YORK - The United Nations has announced plans to reduce its global peacekeeping force by 25%, a move prompted by significant U.S. funding cuts under President Donald Trump’s foreign aid reduction plan.

According to a senior UN official, between 13,000 and 14,000 troops and police officers will be withdrawn from the organization’s nine active peacekeeping missions in the coming months. The cuts will impact several regions, including Africa and the Middle East, with the Somalia mission among those expected to be most affected.

Currently, the UN maintains around 50,000 uniformed personnel across its peacekeeping operations. The new directive also includes a 15% reduction in the UN’s military budget for the current fiscal year, as part of broader cost-saving measures.

The largest missions - including those in the Democratic Republic of Congo (MONUSCO), the Central African Republic (MINUSCA), South Sudan (UNMISS), Lebanon (UNIFIL), Cyprus (UNFICYP), and Kosovo (UNMIK) - are expected to undergo significant troop drawdowns.

The decision comes amid growing concerns about the impact of reduced peacekeeping capacity on conflict zones already facing instability and humanitarian crises. Analysts warn that troop cuts could weaken fragile security gains and limit the UN’s ability to protect civilians in volatile regions.

Despite these concerns, UN leadership has defended the move as a necessary adjustment to shifting global priorities and funding realities, emphasizing that peacebuilding and local capacity-building efforts will remain central to the organization’s mission.

title: Shield Tech Hub Leads Rwanda’s Fight Against Cybercrime
excerpt: Kigali, Rwanda - Shield Tech Hub, a Rwandan cybersecurity company based at Norrsken House Kigali, is gaining recognition for its innovative approach to fighting cybercrime.
title_en: Shield Tech Hub Leads Rwanda’s Fight Against Cybercrime
excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda - Shield Tech Hub, a Rwandan cybersecurity company based at Norrsken House Kigali, is gaining recognition for its innovative approach to fighting cybercrime.
body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda - Shield Tech Hub, a Rwandan cybersecurity company based at Norrsken House Kigali, is gaining recognition for its innovative approach to fighting cybercrime. Founded three years ago by technology expert Joel Gashayija, the firm infiltrates cybercriminal networks to uncover their methods and alert Rwandan companies to potential threats before attacks occur.

The company currently serves over 30 public and private organizations, providing digital defense services, security audits, and specialized training. It also collaborates closely with the National Cyber Security Authority (NCSA) to build local expertise.

Shield Tech Hub showcased its work during the launch of the International Model Institute for Cyber Security and Privacy (Cyber Academy) - a new center expected to train more than 200 cybersecurity professionals annually, with women representing at least 30% of trainees.

One of Shield Tech Hub’s signature innovations is Threat Informant, a Rwandan-built system that scans dark web markets to detect leaked corporate data such as passwords, financial information, and internal documents. The system analyzes these threats and provides actionable intelligence to clients, helping them close security gaps.

“When we tell them what cybercriminals are planning, they strengthen their systems and eliminate vulnerabilities,” said Gashayija. “This is homegrown technology built in Rwanda.”

The company’s team of 13 trained young professionals-many recruited as students-has become part of Rwanda’s growing pool of cybersecurity specialists. Yet, Gashayija acknowledges that as cybercriminals evolve their tactics, constant innovation is required to stay ahead.

According to Interpol’s 2025 Cybersecurity Report, cybercrime in East and West Africa has risen by 30% since 2019, costing the continent more than $3 billion. To address these threats, Rwanda is investing in education and capacity-building through initiatives such as the Cyber Academy, the University of Rwanda Coding Academy, and national programs aimed at training one million coding experts and 500,000 advanced technology specialists by 2029.

title: Two Killed, Five Injured in Clashes Between FARDC and Wazalendo Fighters in Kamituga
excerpt: At least two people were killed and five others injured following two days of fighting between government forces and members of the pro-government Wazalendo coalition in Kamituga, a mining town in South Kivu province…
title_en: Two Killed, Five Injured in Clashes Between FARDC and Wazalendo Fighters in Kamituga
excerpt_en: At least two people were killed and five others injured following two days of fighting between government forces and members of the pro-government Wazalendo coalition in Kamituga, a mining town in South Kivu province…
body_en:
At least two people were killed and five others injured following two days of fighting between government forces and members of the pro-government Wazalendo coalition in Kamituga, a mining town in South Kivu province, eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

According to local civil society sources, calm returned on the morning of October 11, 2025, after heavy gunfire had rattled the southern part of Kamituga the previous evening.

Jean Pierre Le Mwanda, head of the Kamituga civil society platform, confirmed the casualties, saying:

“Two people died in the fighting - one FARDC soldier and the town’s police chief - while five civilians were injured.”

The clashes reportedly began on the evening of October 9, when a Wazalendo fighter shot and killed a soldier from the Congolese Armed Forces (FARDC). The incident sparked protests as residents carried the soldier’s body through the streets, demanding the withdrawal of Wazalendo fighters from the area.

Fighting resumed the following day, spreading toward the southern parts of Kamituga near the offices of the National Institute for the Conservation of Nature (ICCN). Witnesses reported that Wazalendo fighters looted several local shops during the violence.

The Kamituga city administration confirmed the death toll and said the local Security Council, chaired by Mayor Alexandre Bundya Mpila, had met to assess the situation and dispatched teams to affected neighborhoods for “consolation and reassurance tours.”

“The situation has now stabilized, but the city remains under close surveillance,” a municipal official said.

The Wazalendo (“patriots”) groups are a loose coalition of armed militias that pledged to support the Congolese army against the M23 rebellion. However, relations between the FARDC and some Wazalendo factions have grown tense in recent months, with repeated reports of clashes over control of territory, taxation points, and local governance.

Observers say the Kamituga incident underscores the growing fragility of the alliance between the FARDC and local self-defense groups, complicating government efforts to stabilize eastern Congo amid ongoing insurgencies and peace negotiations.

The declaration was made on October 9, 2025, as Busu presented a power transformer to residents of Kamanyola commune in Walungu territory.

Speaking to residents, the governor said AFC/M23 remains committed to what he described as the removal of a “corrupt” government led by President Félix Tshisekedi and urged locals to join the coalition. He said the group’s commander‑in‑chief, Gen. Maj. Sultani Makenga, had instructed him to tell Kamanyola inhabitants that “in a few days we will go and capture Uvira.”

The pronouncement comes amid ongoing clashes across parts of South Kivu, where AFC/M23 has been fighting local militias and ad hoc armed groups. The coalition claims recent advances in areas near Shabunda and Mwenga, including the capture of Chulwe, Kintuluku and Lubimbe, the statement said.

Local defense forces in and around Uvira are reported to include elements of the FARDC (DRC armed forces) as well as Burundian contingents and Wazalendo militias aligned with commanders such as William Yakutumba and John Makanaki. Those forces have publicly pledged to repel any attempt by AFC/M23 to enter the city.

In a public appeal, AFC/M23 leader Prof. Stanislas Baleke addressed rival commanders directly, urging them to abandon what he termed the “wagon of lies” propagated by Kinshasa and to withdraw from Uvira to avoid casualties. “My brothers Makanaki, Kamama, Yakutumba, Ngoma Nzito, all of you, run away quickly when you hear the first shot… I do not want you to die,” Baleke said.

The threat to Uvira - a strategic port town on the western shore of Lake Tanganyika - raises fears among residents about potential escalation, displacement and disruptions to trade and humanitarian access. Kamanyola, where the governor spoke, sits along a corridor frequently affected by rebel movements and inter‑group clashes.

Observers tracking the conflict note that alliances in eastern DRC are fluid: militias once allied with government forces have clashed with the FARDC or switched sides, creating complex fronts and localized tensions. The latest AFC/M23 declaration underscores the fragility of security in parts of South Kivu and the persistent risk of broader confrontations.

Local authorities in Kamanyola said the governor’s visit included community outreach and material support, but the security council and municipal leaders are also said to be monitoring the troop movements closely and coordinating measures to protect civilians.

title: AFC/M23 Says Kagame Not Responsible for Its Actions Amid Tshisekedi Criticism
excerpt: Bertrand Bisimwa, Deputy Leader of the AFC/M23 in charge of political affairs, has strongly rejected President Félix Tshisekedi’s repeated comparisons of Rwandan President Paul Kagame to the rebel coalition.
title_en: AFC/M23 Says Kagame Not Responsible for Its Actions Amid Tshisekedi Criticism
excerpt_en: Bertrand Bisimwa, Deputy Leader of the AFC/M23 in charge of political affairs, has strongly rejected President Félix Tshisekedi’s repeated comparisons of Rwandan President Paul Kagame to the rebel coalition.
body_en:
Bertrand Bisimwa, Deputy Leader of the AFC/M23 in charge of political affairs, has strongly rejected President Félix Tshisekedi’s repeated comparisons of Rwandan President Paul Kagame to the rebel coalition.

Speaking after the EU-Africa Global Gateway Summit on October 9, 2025, Tshisekedi accused Rwanda of backing M23 fighters - allegations Kigali has consistently denied. Portraying himself as a peacemaker, Tshisekedi urged Rwandans and Congolese to live in peace, but stressed that this would depend on the cessation of hostilities by the M23, which currently controls large swaths of eastern DRC.

“This requires you to order the M23 forces, supported by your country, to stop this deadly fighting,” Tshisekedi told Kagame.

In response, President Kagame dismissed the remarks on X (formerly Twitter), using a local proverb to suggest the accusations were empty, saying:

“If someone has a problem with the noise of an empty barrel, he too has a problem! It’s better to let it pass or take it far away!”

Bisimwa clarified that Tshisekedi’s call for reconciliation concerns the governments of Rwanda and the DRC, not the AFC/M23. He emphasized that the coalition expects Tshisekedi to honor promises made directly to it:

“The reconciliation Tshisekedi requested from Kagame concerns both countries, but it does not concern us. We are waiting for him to reconcile with the AFC/M23, starting with fulfilling the promises he gave us. One should not talk about the hand when he does not fulfill anything.”

The roots of the current crisis trace back to November 2021, when M23 fighters resumed hostilities after Tshisekedi refused to integrate them into the national security apparatus despite prior agreements during 14 months of Kinshasa negotiations. Integration was meant to stabilize eastern DRC, home to over 200 armed groups.

While Tshisekedi had long labeled M23 as a terrorist group, the rebels’ capture of Goma and Bukavu in early 2025 pressured him into reluctantly agreeing to negotiations. Since March 2025, Qatar has hosted talks between the DRC government and AFC/M23, but persistent fighting in North and South Kivu has hindered progress.

Benjamin Mbonimpa, Permanent Secretary of AFC/M23, warned that Tshisekedi’s statements make it “a serious problem” to send a delegation to Doha for discussions next week. The Qatari-hosted talks are expected to focus on ceasefire measures and frameworks for a lasting peace agreement between the two sides.

title: South Kivu: Deadly Clashes Erupt Among Wazalendo Groups in Uvira and Fizi
excerpt: Internal clashes among Wazalendo self-defense groups in South Kivu province, eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, left several people dead and others injured on Thursday, October 16, 2025, according to local civil…
title_en: South Kivu: Deadly Clashes Erupt Among Wazalendo Groups in Uvira and Fizi
excerpt_en: Internal clashes among Wazalendo self-defense groups in South Kivu province, eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, left several people dead and others injured on Thursday, October 16, 2025, according to local civil…
body_en:
Internal clashes among Wazalendo self-defense groups in South Kivu province, eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, left several people dead and others injured on Thursday, October 16, 2025, according to local civil society sources.

In Uvira territory, a faction led by a self-proclaimed commander known as “General Nyerere” exchanged fire with another group led by “General Makanaki” in the Biriba area of Runingu commune, leaving three people injured.

In a separate incident in Luvungi-Itara, also in Uvira, rival factions led by individuals identified as Kiyaye and Kangadadi clashed, injuring one person, civil society representatives said.

Fighting also spread to neighboring Fizi territory. In Kikonde commune, two rival wings of the Mai-Mai Biloze Bishambuke group turned on each other, resulting in the death of a senior Wazalendo fighter. The incident caused panic in the area.

“The commander died instantly and panic followed. All activities came to a halt as residents chose to stay indoors,” said a civil society member based in Fizi.

In another violent episode the same day, clashes in the Mutambala area of the Basimukuma Sud commune led to the killing of a young girl and her mother.

Local leaders have expressed concern over the continued insecurity caused by infighting among Wazalendo groups, who were initially mobilized to support government forces against foreign-backed rebel movements.

Mafikiri Mashimangou, head of a civil society organization operating in Uvira and Fizi, warned that instability in the Ruzizi Valley is worsening due to repeated confrontations.

“The provincial authorities must urgently convene a special security meeting with Wazalendo leaders operating in the Ruzizi Valley to coordinate their activities and prevent further bloodshed,” he said.

Uvira’s deputy territory administrator, Kifaru Kibonge Decky, confirmed that security officials held a crisis meeting on October 16 and discussed measures to prevent further clashes.

Despite the recent efforts, residents say fear remains high as rival militia groups continue to operate freely in the region, threatening fragile security gains.

title: South Kivu: Burundi Deploys More Troops to Counter AFC/M23 Advance
excerpt: Burundi has reinforced its military presence in South Kivu province in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) to push back advancing AFC/M23 rebels, according to local sources and regional media reports.
title_en: South Kivu: Burundi Deploys More Troops to Counter AFC/M23 Advance
excerpt_en: Burundi has reinforced its military presence in South Kivu province in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) to push back advancing AFC/M23 rebels, according to local sources and regional media reports.
body_en:
Burundi has reinforced its military presence in South Kivu province in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) to push back advancing AFC/M23 rebels, according to local sources and regional media reports.

In recent days, convoys of Burundian troops have been seen heading toward strategic zones in the territories of Uvira, Fizi and Mwenga, where clashes have intensified. According to SOS Médias Burundi, military trucks carrying Burundian soldiers were spotted in Kitoga, Muhuzi and Itombwe forest, with additional deployments reported in Minembwe, Mikalati, Kipupu and Point Zero in Fizi territory.

The deployments come after AFC/M23 fighters seized several localities in South Kivu over the past two weeks, including Luntukulu, Chulwe, Kishadu and Lubimbe, while also launching attacks on Mwenga and Shabunda town centers.

Military sources say the new Burundian reinforcements aim to prevent the rebels from advancing further toward Uvira, a key economic and strategic hub along Lake Tanganyika.

There are also unconfirmed reports that Burundian troops are preparing operations against positions held by Twirwaneho, a local armed group in the Mikenke area of Minembwe accused of collaborating with AFC/M23.

The escalation comes just days after the DRC government and AFC/M23 signed a commitment on October 14, 2025, to establish a joint mechanism for monitoring a ceasefire. The new movements by Burundian forces suggest a potential shift in military strategy, raising questions about the future of the truce.

Burundi’s military has been operating in eastern DRC since 2022 under a bilateral security agreement renewed in 2023. Estimates suggest around 20,000 Burundian soldiers are currently deployed in South Kivu, mainly in Uvira and Fizi territories, to support Congolese forces against rebel groups.

Neither the Burundian nor Congolese governments have officially commented on the recent troop movements. However, security analysts warn that a widening regional military intervention could risk further destabilizing the volatile Great Lakes region.

title: DRC Army Clashes with Wazalendo Fighters in Maniema
excerpt: The Democratic Republic of Congo’s army (FARDC) clashed with Wazalendo alliance fighters in Nyanga village, Punia Center, Maniema Province, on October 14, 2025, forcing residents to stay indoors for over an hour, local…
title_en: DRC Army Clashes with Wazalendo Fighters in Maniema
excerpt_en: The Democratic Republic of Congo’s army (FARDC) clashed with Wazalendo alliance fighters in Nyanga village, Punia Center, Maniema Province, on October 14, 2025, forcing residents to stay indoors for over an hour, local…
body_en:
The Democratic Republic of Congo’s army (FARDC) clashed with Wazalendo alliance fighters in Nyanga village, Punia Center, Maniema Province, on October 14, 2025, forcing residents to stay indoors for over an hour, local authorities said.

The Punia territorial commander, Ndarabu Abedi, reported that the fighting involved a Wazalendo faction led by a self-styled Colonel Serpent. “FARDC and Wazalendo often clash in Punia. Today, the situation escalated, and fighting broke out during the day,” he said.

Commander Ndarabu noted that similar confrontations occurred last month, resulting in multiple deaths at a roadblock set up by Wazalendo fighters.

Historically, clashes between FARDC and Wazalendo in Maniema are not new. In August 2024, fighters led by Amani Useni Josué, known as Saddam, attacked DRC forces in Kindu, leaving nine people dead.

Authorities continue to monitor the situation as tensions persist between government forces and local armed groups in Punia and surrounding areas.

title: DRC Forces Launch Attacks on AFC/M23 Positions Despite Ceasefire Agreement
excerpt: The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government forces launched military operations against AFC/M23 coalition positions in North and South Kivu just hours after both parties signed a ceasefire agreement in Doha…
title_en: DRC Forces Launch Attacks on AFC/M23 Positions Despite Ceasefire Agreement
excerpt_en: The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government forces launched military operations against AFC/M23 coalition positions in North and South Kivu just hours after both parties signed a ceasefire agreement in Doha…
body_en:
The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government forces launched military operations against AFC/M23 coalition positions in North and South Kivu just hours after both parties signed a ceasefire agreement in Doha, Qatar, on October 14, 2025, the rebel group said.

AFC/M23 spokesman Lawrence Kanyuka stated on the morning of October 15, 2025, that the attacks involved FARDC-affiliated militias, including the Wazalendo coalition, targeting densely populated areas and key rebel positions.

“The Kinshasa government forces carried out major assaults on our positions in South and North Kivu, shortly after the signing of the Doha ceasefire agreement,” Kanyuka said.

Specific locations under attack included Kadasomwa and Lumbishi in Kalehe territory, South Kivu, and Kasake in Masisi territory, North Kivu.

The ceasefire agreement in Doha established a joint monitoring body composed of equal representatives from the DRC government and AFC/M23, with observers from the United States, Qatar, African Union, and the Great Lakes Region. The body is intended to oversee compliance and facilitate ongoing peace negotiations.

Kanyuka warned that the attacks not only endanger civilians but also threaten the progress of the peace process, potentially undermining efforts to reach a lasting agreement between the two sides.

Analysts say the situation highlights the fragility of ceasefires in eastern DRC, where ongoing clashes between government forces and rebel groups continue to challenge regional stability.

This report illustrates a marked contrast between Rwanda's domestic situation and the tense regional context in which the country operates. Internally, Rwanda is demonstrating sustained development momentum, marked by strategic investments in road infrastructure, health (with EU support for vaccine production), and local economic empowerment, particularly for women and SMEs.

However, this progress is overshadowed by persistent tensions with the Democratic Republic of Congo. Despite attempts at dialogue within the Washington and Doha peace processes, deep mistrust persists. Mutual accusations between Presidents Tshisekedi and Kagame, contradictions within the Congolese government itself, and, above all, the extremely volatile security situation in eastern DRC-with clashes involving the M23, the Congolese army, and various militias-continue to threaten regional stability.

In summary, while Rwanda is consolidating its economic and social development, its geopolitical environment remains precarious, with the resolution of the conflict in eastern DRC being the key to lasting peace in the Great Lakes region.

title: Rwanda, U.S. Deepen Cooperation on Nuclear Energy and Critical Minerals
excerpt: Rwanda and the United States have strengthened their partnership in the fields of nuclear energy, mineral development, and energy innovation following high-level talks held in Washington, D.C.
title_en: Rwanda, U.S. Deepen Cooperation on Nuclear Energy and Critical Minerals
excerpt_en: Rwanda and the United States have strengthened their partnership in the fields of nuclear energy, mineral development, and energy innovation following high-level talks held in Washington, D.C.
body_en:
Rwanda and the United States have strengthened their partnership in the fields of nuclear energy, mineral development, and energy innovation following high-level talks held in Washington, D.C.

Prime Minister Dr. Justin Nsengiyumva met with U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright to discuss new areas of collaboration, including the peaceful use of nuclear energy, natural gas development, and the exploration and processing of key minerals essential to global clean energy transitions.

Dr. Nsengiyumva was in the United States to attend a dinner organized by the International Conservation Caucus Foundation (ICCF), where discussions also touched on sustainable energy policies and climate resilience.

The meeting builds on Rwanda’s growing engagement in the global nuclear energy community. In September 2025, Dr. Fidel Ndahayo, Director General of the Rwanda Atomic Energy Board (RAEB), announced that Rwanda is prioritizing several projects under the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) framework to expand the peaceful use of nuclear technology.

Among these initiatives is the “Rays of Hope” project, designed to enhance the use of nuclear energy in medicine-particularly in diagnosing and treating cancer and other serious diseases. The “Atoms4Water” project focuses on using nuclear science to monitor and improve water quality, as well as to locate underground water sources. Another program, “ZODIAC” (Zoonotic Disease Integrated Action), aims to strengthen early detection and response to zoonotic diseases that can spread from animals to humans.

To support these ambitions, Rwanda plans to establish the Center for Nuclear Science and Technology (CNST) in Bugesera District, near the Rwanda Institute for Conservation Agriculture (RICA). The facility will serve as a hub for nuclear research, training, and innovation.

The country also intends to adopt Small Modular Reactors (SMRs)-a new generation of compact, efficient nuclear power plants. According to Dr. Ndahayo, Rwanda has already committed to training 234 nuclear energy experts by 2028, paving the way for the installation of its first SMR plant by 2030.

In addition, Rwanda is preparing to deploy Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scanners to enhance nuclear medicine services in local hospitals. To ensure safety and compliance, the government continues to strengthen its independent nuclear regulatory authority, responsible for oversight and risk management in the sector.

Dr. Ndahayo emphasized that these initiatives are part of Rwanda’s long-term strategy to promote science-driven industrialization, encourage technology transfer, and position the country as a regional model in clean energy innovation.

For Rwanda to achieve its Vision 2050-becoming a high-income, developed nation-it will need to generate at least five gigawatts of electricity. Nuclear energy, he said, will play a key role in meeting that target by providing reliable and sustainable power.

Electricity generated from nuclear energy relies on the process of nuclear fission, where uranium atoms are split to release heat. This heat is then used to produce steam, which drives turbines to generate electricity inside a nuclear reactor-the heart of the power plant.

Through continued collaboration with international partners such as the United States and the IAEA, Rwanda aims to harness the potential of nuclear science to power its development, improve healthcare, and advance technological innovation across multiple sectors.
body_fr:
Rwanda and the United States have strengthened their partnership in the fields of nuclear energy, mineral development, and energy innovation following high-level talks held in Washington, D.C.

Prime Minister Dr. Justin Nsengiyumva met with U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright to discuss new areas of collaboration, including the peaceful use of nuclear energy, natural gas development, and the exploration and processing of key minerals essential to global clean energy transitions.

Dr. Nsengiyumva was in the United States to attend a dinner organized by the International Conservation Caucus Foundation (ICCF), where discussions also touched on sustainable energy policies and climate resilience.

The meeting builds on Rwanda’s growing engagement in the global nuclear energy community. In September 2025, Dr. Fidel Ndahayo, Director General of the Rwanda Atomic Energy Board (RAEB), announced that Rwanda is prioritizing several projects under the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) framework to expand the peaceful use of nuclear technology.

Among these initiatives is the “Rays of Hope” project, designed to enhance the use of nuclear energy in medicine-particularly in diagnosing and treating cancer and other serious diseases. The “Atoms4Water” project focuses on using nuclear science to monitor and improve water quality, as well as to locate underground water sources. Another program, “ZODIAC” (Zoonotic Disease Integrated Action), aims to strengthen early detection and response to zoonotic diseases that can spread from animals to humans.

To support these ambitions, Rwanda plans to establish the Center for Nuclear Science and Technology (CNST) in Bugesera District, near the Rwanda Institute for Conservation Agriculture (RICA). The facility will serve as a hub for nuclear research, training, and innovation.

The country also intends to adopt Small Modular Reactors (SMRs)-a new generation of compact, efficient nuclear power plants. According to Dr. Ndahayo, Rwanda has already committed to training 234 nuclear energy experts by 2028, paving the way for the installation of its first SMR plant by 2030.

In addition, Rwanda is preparing to deploy Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scanners to enhance nuclear medicine services in local hospitals. To ensure safety and compliance, the government continues to strengthen its independent nuclear regulatory authority, responsible for oversight and risk management in the sector.

Dr. Ndahayo emphasized that these initiatives are part of Rwanda’s long-term strategy to promote science-driven industrialization, encourage technology transfer, and position the country as a regional model in clean energy innovation.

For Rwanda to achieve its Vision 2050-becoming a high-income, developed nation-it will need to generate at least five gigawatts of electricity. Nuclear energy, he said, will play a key role in meeting that target by providing reliable and sustainable power.

Electricity generated from nuclear energy relies on the process of nuclear fission, where uranium atoms are split to release heat. This heat is then used to produce steam, which drives turbines to generate electricity inside a nuclear reactor-the heart of the power plant.

Through continued collaboration with international partners such as the United States and the IAEA, Rwanda aims to harness the potential of nuclear science to power its development, improve healthcare, and advance technological innovation across multiple sectors.

title: Rwanda Reaffirms Link Between Peace, Development, and Environmental Protection
excerpt: Rwanda’s Prime Minister, Dr. Justin Nsengiyumva, has emphasized that lasting peace and sustainable development are inseparable from environmental protection, urging nations to safeguard their natural ecosystems from…
title_en: Rwanda Reaffirms Link Between Peace, Development, and Environmental Protection
excerpt_en: Rwanda’s Prime Minister, Dr. Justin Nsengiyumva, has emphasized that lasting peace and sustainable development are inseparable from environmental protection, urging nations to safeguard their natural ecosystems from…
body_en:
Rwanda’s Prime Minister, Dr. Justin Nsengiyumva, has emphasized that lasting peace and sustainable development are inseparable from environmental protection, urging nations to safeguard their natural ecosystems from terrorism and illegal activities.

Speaking during a high-level meeting hosted by the International Conservation Caucus Foundation (ICCF) in the United States, Dr. Nsengiyumva underscored the importance of placing environmental conservation at the heart of national development strategies.

“Peace and development cannot be sustained without continuing to protect the environment, on which our people depend for their livelihoods,” he said. “That is why Rwanda has placed environmental protection at the forefront of its development strategies for nearly three decades.”

The ICCF meeting gathered over 200 participants, including members of parliament, international leaders, conservationists, representatives of investment firms, NGOs, and public figures. Since its launch in 2006, the forum has hosted notable figures such as King Charles III, Jeff Bezos, Queen Noor of Jordan, Prince Albert II of Monaco, and former U.S. Presidents George H. W. Bush and Bill Clinton.

Dr. Nsengiyumva highlighted Rwanda’s post-Genocide recovery efforts, particularly in biodiversity restoration and wildlife conservation. He pointed to the country’s flagship annual event, Kwita Izina, which celebrates the naming of baby gorillas - a practice that has strengthened conservation awareness and boosted tourism.

“There was a time when mountain gorillas were so endangered that it seemed they might disappear completely. Today, their number has grown to over 1,000 - a fourfold increase - and they are no longer considered endangered,” he noted.

Rwanda’s partnership with African Parks to manage Akagera National Park has also yielded remarkable results. Since the collaboration began 15 years ago, the park’s animal population has grown from fewer than 5,000 to nearly 12,000. The country also successfully reintroduced lions in 2015 and later brought back black and white rhinos, a feat achieved with the support of the Howard G. Buffett Foundation.

Dr. Nsengiyumva stressed that such conservation successes would not be possible without the involvement of local communities, who serve as the first line of defense for protected areas.

The Prime Minister cautioned African nations against allowing national parks to become safe havens for terrorist or criminal groups, warning that such activities undermine both peace and environmental sustainability.

“We cannot allow African parks to be used by terrorist groups and criminal networks to create insecurity,” he asserted.

He also expressed appreciation to the United States, acknowledging the role of former President Donald Trump in facilitating peace efforts between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), saying that continued cooperation would help preserve regional ecosystems.

Dr. Nsengiyumva concluded by reaffirming Rwanda’s commitment to conservation and announcing plans to establish the African Conservation Academy in Akagera National Park, an initiative aimed at building continental expertise in biodiversity protection and sustainable development.

title: Rwandan Ambassador Vincent Karega Presents Credentials in Algeria
excerpt: Ambassador Vincent Karega, Rwanda’s first resident envoy to Algeria, officially presented his credentials to President Abdelmadjid Tebboune, marking a significant step in strengthening bilateral ties between the two countries.
title_en: Rwandan Ambassador Vincent Karega Presents Credentials in Algeria
excerpt_en: Ambassador Vincent Karega, Rwanda’s first resident envoy to Algeria, officially presented his credentials to President Abdelmadjid Tebboune, marking a significant step in strengthening bilateral ties between the two countries.
body_en:
Ambassador Vincent Karega, Rwanda’s first resident envoy to Algeria, officially presented his credentials to President Abdelmadjid Tebboune, marking a significant step in strengthening bilateral ties between the two countries. The announcement was shared on October 28, 2025, via the X platform.

“I am pleased to present my credentials to President Tebboune of Algeria as the first Rwandan Ambassador to reside in this country. Rwanda and Algeria are committed to working together to strengthen bilateral relations and enhance cooperation in all areas,” Karega said.

Ambassador Karega joins other diplomats presenting credentials to President Tebboune, including representatives from Bangladesh, Austria, Sweden, Ukraine, and Egypt.

Rwanda and Algeria maintain cooperation in security and education, with Rwandan students pursuing studies in the Arabic, French, and Tamazight-speaking country. Since 1982, the two nations have signed agreements covering economic, social, cultural, and cooperative sectors.

In December 2023, Algeria opened its embassy in Kigali, reflecting both nations’ commitment to deepening relations. Earlier, on June 3, 2025, President Paul Kagame visited Algeria, touring the National School of Artificial Intelligence, a leading institution attended by Rwandan students, and holding talks with President Tebboune on cross-border trade and knowledge sharing.

Ambassador Karega previously represented Rwanda in South Africa until 2019, then in the Democratic Republic of the Congo until October 31, 2022, when he left amid strained bilateral relations. On December 20, 2024, he was appointed Special Ambassador in charge of the Great Lakes Region.

His current posting in Algeria is seen as a milestone in expanding Rwanda-Algeria diplomatic and cooperative engagement.

title: Rwanda to Launch $70 Million Digital Identity Card Project
excerpt: The Ministry of Technology and Innovation has announced that the Digital Identity Card Project will cost over $70 million (more than 101 billion Rwf) to complete.
title_en: Rwanda to Launch $70 Million Digital Identity Card Project
excerpt_en: The Ministry of Technology and Innovation has announced that the Digital Identity Card Project will cost over $70 million (more than 101 billion Rwf) to complete.
body_en:
The Ministry of Technology and Innovation has announced that the Digital Identity Card Project will cost over $70 million (more than 101 billion Rwf) to complete. The initiative, which began in 2023, aims to modernize the national identity system and expand access to services for all residents.

Minister of Technology and Innovation, Ingabire Paula, stated that the World Bank has contributed over $48 million (69 billion Rwf) toward building the system but emphasized that additional funding is required to fully implement the project.

“There is a need to build a system and update services that were previously provided to citizens based on their identity cards, so they can start using the electronic identity card,” Minister Ingabire said in an interview with RBA.

The electronic ID card will be issued not only to Rwandans aged 16 and above, but also to foreign residents, refugees, asylum seekers, unaccompanied minors, temporary residents, migrants, and stateless people.

Unlike the traditional ID, the new card will have a QR code that can be carried digitally on a phone or computer, alongside a unique token number to access personal information. This will eliminate the need to carry a physical card when requesting services such as opening bank accounts.

The National Identity Agency (NIDA) has already registered over 3,300 people through a pre-enrollment platform, designed to verify identities and correct errors before issuing the electronic cards. The program officially launched on August 7, 2025, at the Kigali International Fair and will continue at the Indangamirwa Church, before expanding nationwide to districts including Huye, Gisagara, and Nyanza.

Two centers have been set up in each sector, staffed by trained personnel to assist residents with identity verification and documentation, including fingerprints and facial recognition. Currently, 1,144 workers have been trained, with plans to expand to 2,500 by May 2026.

The new ID card will reduce the data collected from 27 categories to nine essential data sets, including names, parents’ names, contact information, and place of birth, ensuring a complete and streamlined identity system.

Minister Ingabire added that by May 2026, Rwanda is expected to become the first African country to implement a fully operational digital ID card, ahead of other nations still in the development phase.

The project has been allocated 5.4 billion Rwf for 2024/2025 and 12.2 billion Rwf for 2025/2026, with additional donor support being sought to ensure nationwide rollout.

This digital ID system is expected to enhance access to public and private services, improve efficiency, and strengthen national identity management across Rwanda.

title: Rwandan Heritage Abroad Still Predominantly in Belgium and Germany, Says Cultural Council Chair
excerpt: KIGALI - Ambassador Masozera Robert, Chairperson of the Cultural Council, has revealed that over 90% of Rwandan cultural heritage remains in countries that colonized Rwanda, notably Belgium and Germany.
title_en: Rwandan Heritage Abroad Still Predominantly in Belgium and Germany, Says Cultural Council Chair
excerpt_en: KIGALI - Ambassador Masozera Robert, Chairperson of the Cultural Council, has revealed that over 90% of Rwandan cultural heritage remains in countries that colonized Rwanda, notably Belgium and Germany.
body_en:
KIGALI - Ambassador Masozera Robert, Chairperson of the Cultural Council, has revealed that over 90% of Rwandan cultural heritage remains in countries that colonized Rwanda, notably Belgium and Germany. He made the remarks on October 27, 2025, during Rwanda’s celebration of the International Day for the Protection of Audiovisual Heritage.

Celebrated for the fifth time in Rwanda, this year’s theme was “Heritage in audio and visual, a channel for the culture and history of Rwandans.” The day provides an opportunity to reflect on the significance of audiovisual materials in preserving and showcasing the diversity of cultural histories worldwide.

Amb. Masozera emphasized the importance of safeguarding Rwanda’s history, noting that audio and visual heritage requires careful preservation. “The history we have here contains a great wealth of documents including photographs, images and sounds that show how Rwanda has developed, but we still need to receive more because what we have is not enough,” he said.

He reiterated that a large portion of Rwanda’s cultural assets were removed during colonial times, stating, “The colonialists, especially Belgium, exploited us… up to 90% of Rwanda's cultural heritage.”

Recent efforts have seen some materials return to Rwanda. In 2021, Belgium, through a partnership with the Royal Museum for Central Africa, donated heritage items including audio recordings such as poems from 1950 to 2007. The previous year, Belgium also returned over 10,000 documents detailing research on Rwanda’s mineral locations dating back to 1923.

The celebration underscored the ongoing need to preserve and recover Rwanda’s rich audio and visual heritage, which reflects the nation’s history, culture, and identity.

title: Habimana Kizito Among 67 EAC Observers Deployed for Tanzania Presidential Elections
excerpt: DAR ES SALAAM - Rwanda’s Habimana Kizito, Vice-Chairperson of the National Electoral Commission, is among 67 observers deployed by the East African Community (EAC) to monitor the Tanzania presidential elections…
title_en: Habimana Kizito Among 67 EAC Observers Deployed for Tanzania Presidential Elections
excerpt_en: DAR ES SALAAM - Rwanda’s Habimana Kizito, Vice-Chairperson of the National Electoral Commission, is among 67 observers deployed by the East African Community (EAC) to monitor the Tanzania presidential elections…
body_en:
DAR ES SALAAM - Rwanda’s Habimana Kizito, Vice-Chairperson of the National Electoral Commission, is among 67 observers deployed by the East African Community (EAC) to monitor the Tanzania presidential elections scheduled for October 29, 2025.

The deployment follows an invitation from the Tanzanian government and aligns with directives from the EAC Council of Ministers, which tasked the EAC Secretariat with observing elections across member states to promote democracy, peace, and regional stability.

Dr. Speciosa Wandira Kazibwe, former Vice President of Uganda (1994-2003) and Director of EAC election observation missions, emphasized the importance of fair elections, stating, “The conduct of fair and transparent elections is the key to democracy and regional unity.”

The observer team includes experts from all eight EAC member states, members of the EAC Legislative Assembly (EALA), representatives of electoral and human rights commissions, civil society organizations, and EAC offices.

Observers will monitor all stages of the electoral process, including campaigning, voting, vote counting, and post-election reporting. Their work is guided by Article 6(d) of the EAC Treaty, which obliges member states to uphold good governance, democracy, human rights, equality, proportionality, integrity, and respect for constitutional processes.

title: RDC Begins Accepting FDLR Surrenders Amid Tensions with AFC/M23
excerpt: KINSHASA, DRC - The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) have begun receiving surrenders from the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), signaling a potential end to military…
title_en: RDC Begins Accepting FDLR Surrenders Amid Tensions with AFC/M23
excerpt_en: KINSHASA, DRC - The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) have begun receiving surrenders from the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), signaling a potential end to military…
body_en:
KINSHASA, DRC - The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) have begun receiving surrenders from the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), signaling a potential end to military operations against the group, which has initiated a process of disarmament.

FARDC spokesperson, Major General Sylvain Ekenge Bomusa, called on FDLR fighters on October 10, 2025, to surrender either to Congolese authorities or to the UN peacekeeping mission, MONUSCO. He warned that those refusing to comply would face military action, in accordance with the Washington Peace Agreement signed in June.

During the third meeting of the Joint Rwanda-DRC Security Council in Washington on October 21-22, officials from both countries, alongside U.S. and observer representatives, confirmed that while most FDLR fighters had yet to disarm, some had started the process, according to General Ekenge.

In an interview with Deutsche Welle journalist Wendy Bashi, General Ekenge stated that “the FDLR have followed the instructions of the Congolese army.” He added that the group is currently located in areas controlled by the AFC/M23 coalition in Rutshuru territory, North Kivu, which has hindered their ability to reach Congolese authorities or MONUSCO to formally surrender.

“Others have prevented them from laying down their arms,” General Ekenge said. “They want to surrender, but obstacles in AFC/M23-controlled zones have delayed this process.” He added that FARDC would continue its campaign to facilitate the group’s surrender.

The general acknowledged that the reasons behind AFC/M23’s obstruction remain unclear but reaffirmed the army’s commitment to encouraging FDLR fighters to disarm. “We are carrying out the tasks assigned to us. We have conducted a campaign within the FDLR to urge surrender, and we will continue,” he said.

Tensions persist over the implementation of the Washington Agreement, which includes provisions for information sharing on FDLR operations and affiliates. Rwanda and the DRC had agreed to exchange intelligence on potential threats, military capabilities, locations of units, and weaponry.

In July 2025, Rwanda’s Foreign Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe reported that some FDLR combatants had been recruited into the Congolese army and Wazalendo, with their positions known to Kigali. “We have all the information on the FDLR, including their locations and units. They cannot feign ignorance,” Nduhungirehe said.

Rwanda’s Financial Intelligence Centre (FIC), when listing 25 Rwandans as terrorists on October 25, indicated that top FDLR leaders remained in Walikale as of October 14. These include FDLR president Gaston Iyamuremye, alias Lt. Gen. Byiringiro Victor, and group leader Pacifique Ntawunga, alias Gen. Omega, both residing in the Buhaya neighborhood of Walikale.

The unfolding situation highlights the complex dynamics between the FDLR, FARDC, and AFC/M23, raising questions about the effective disarmament of the group and the security situation in North Kivu.

title: Six New Senators Sworn In as Rwanda Welcomes Fresh Appointments and Returning Members
excerpt: KIGALI, Rwanda - On October 24, 2025, the Rwandan Senate welcomed six new members, including four presidential appointees and two elected representatives, strengthening the upper chamber with a mix of experience and…
title_en: Six New Senators Sworn In as Rwanda Welcomes Fresh Appointments and Returning Members
excerpt_en: KIGALI, Rwanda - On October 24, 2025, the Rwandan Senate welcomed six new members, including four presidential appointees and two elected representatives, strengthening the upper chamber with a mix of experience and…
body_en:
KIGALI, Rwanda - On October 24, 2025, the Rwandan Senate welcomed six new members, including four presidential appointees and two elected representatives, strengthening the upper chamber with a mix of experience and fresh perspectives.

Among those appointed by President Paul Kagame were Dr. Uwamariya Valentine and Alfred Gasana, while Prof. Dusingizemungu Jean Pierre and Uwizeyimana Evode began their second five-year Senate terms. The two senators elected by the Consultative Forum of Legal Political Parties were Dr. Frank Habineza and Alphonse Nkubana.

Dr. Uwamariya Valentine, born May 14, 1971, in Nyamasheke, holds degrees in Organic Chemistry from the former National University of Rwanda, a Master’s in Environmental Engineering and Water Technology from the Netherlands Institute of Technology, and another Master’s from the University of the Witwatersrand, South Africa. She has over 18 years of teaching and research experience, previously serving as Dean of the School of Science at the University of Rwanda and as Vice-Chancellor of Rwanda Polytechnic. Most recently, she held leadership positions in the Ministries of Education, Gender and Family Development, and Environment.

Alfred Gasana, former Member of Parliament and head of the Political Affairs Committee, has held key government roles, including Minister of Security and Rwanda’s Ambassador to the Netherlands. He previously led the Internal Security Department at the National Intelligence and Security Service (NISS).

Prof. Dusingizemungu Jean Pierre, who served as the head of IBUKA for a decade, has a long history in education and public service. Born in 1963, he joined the RPF Inkotanyi in 1992 and became Bourgmestre of Gahini in 1994. He first joined the Senate in 2020 and has now been reappointed for a second term.

Dr. Frank Habineza, born February 22, 1977, in Mityana, Uganda, served as a Member of Parliament from 2018 to 2024, including as Vice Chair of the Human Rights Committee. He has an extensive academic background, holding Master’s degrees in War Studies, Governance, and Democracy and Human Rights, and is currently studying law at the University of Kigali.

Alphonse Nkubana is an entrepreneur and politician with over 25 years of experience in business, governance, and institutional development. Founder of Positive Thinking Ltd, he has served as General Secretary of the PSP and as Spokesperson of the Federation of Legal Political Organizations in Rwanda. Nkubana holds a Master’s in International Relations from Mount Kenya University and a Bachelor’s in Accounting from Kigali Independent University.

Uwizeyimana Evode, born in 1970, began his government career in 2016 as Secretary of State for the Constitution. He participated in the 2015 constitutional review commission and first joined the Senate in 2020. He was reappointed for a second term and sworn in alongside his colleagues on October 24.

Senators in Rwanda are appointed or elected for five-year terms, renewable once, and this cohort is expected to bring a blend of expertise in governance, education, security, law, and entrepreneurship to the legislative body.

title: Minister Nduhungirehe Commends France for Convicting Dr. Munyemana for Genocide Crimes
excerpt: KIGALI, Rwanda - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, has expressed gratitude to the French judiciary for convicting Dr.
title_en: Minister Nduhungirehe Commends France for Convicting Dr. Munyemana for Genocide Crimes
excerpt_en: KIGALI, Rwanda - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, has expressed gratitude to the French judiciary for convicting Dr.
body_en:
KIGALI, Rwanda - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, has expressed gratitude to the French judiciary for convicting Dr. Munyemana Sosthène of his role in the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi.

Dr. Munyemana, a former gynecologist at Butare Hospital affiliated with the former National University of Rwanda, was a respected figure in Tumba Sector and known as a friend of local leaders. However, he was implicated in crimes committed during the genocide, including imprisoning Tutsi victims before they were killed. He claimed his actions were intended to protect them from the Interahamwe militia.

On the night of October 23, 2025, the Appeals Chamber of the French People’s Court upheld his conviction for genocide, crimes against humanity, and complicity in genocide, sentencing him to 24 years in prison. The sentence confirmed the ruling from the trial chamber in December 2023, which Dr. Munyemana had appealed, seeking acquittal and a reduced sentence.

Minister Nduhungirehe praised the decision, stating, “The French judiciary acted with due diligence to provide justice to the victims of the Genocide against the Tutsi, as the Paris Court of Appeal confirmed yesterday when it sentenced Dr. Munyemana Sosthène to 24 years in prison for genocide, crimes against humanity, and complicity in genocide.”

Since 2014, several Rwandans residing in France have been convicted for their involvement in the 1994 genocide. Pascal Simbikangwa, former head of Rwanda’s intelligence service, was sentenced to 25 years in March 2014. In July 2016, Ngenzi Octavien and Tito Barahira, former commune leaders implicated in massacres in Kabarrondo, received life sentences.

In July 2022, Laurent Bucyibaruta, former Prefect of Gikongoro, was sentenced to 20 years for genocide and crimes against humanity. In June 2023, Hategekimana Philippe, a former gendarme involved in the Butare genocide, was sentenced to life imprisonment, with the sentence upheld on appeal in November 2024.

The conviction of Dr. Munyemana marks another step in holding perpetrators accountable and underscores France’s commitment to prosecuting international crimes.

title: Kigali: Minister Marizamunda urges land forces to uphold responsibilities and strengthen cooperation
excerpt: KIGALI, Rwanda - The Minister of Defense, Juvenal Marizamunda, has reminded land force commanders of their critical role in responding to crises and stressed the importance of regional cooperation during the closing of…
title_en: Kigali: Minister Marizamunda urges land forces to uphold responsibilities and strengthen cooperation
excerpt_en: KIGALI, Rwanda - The Minister of Defense, Juvenal Marizamunda, has reminded land force commanders of their critical role in responding to crises and stressed the importance of regional cooperation during the closing of…
body_en:
KIGALI, Rwanda - The Minister of Defense, Juvenal Marizamunda, has reminded land force commanders of their critical role in responding to crises and stressed the importance of regional cooperation during the closing of the two-day “Land Force Commanders Symposium” in Kigali on October 22, 2025.

The international conference, held for the second time following its inaugural meeting in France, brought together military leaders, experts, and stakeholders from across Africa and beyond to discuss continental security challenges and strategies for enhanced cooperation.

In his closing remarks, Minister Marizamunda highlighted the central role of the armed forces in responding to emergencies and maintaining peace. “We are in a difficult time that presents security challenges, including war and cross-border insecurity. The armed forces respond in times of crisis, stop violence, and lay the foundation for peace,” he said.

The symposium underscored Rwanda’s commitment to fostering military cooperation, knowledge sharing, and peacekeeping across the continent. Minister Marizamunda thanked participants for their contributions, emphasizing that joint training and collaborative strategies are essential to building a future of peace and development in Africa.

Rwandan President and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces, Paul Kagame, opened the meeting by calling on African nations to unite in addressing security threats, noting that no continent can rely solely on external solutions. “Cooperation and collaboration based on understanding and mutual respect are what is needed,” he said.

The conference featured senior military figures, including former Nigerian Army Chief of Staff Lt Gen (Rtd) Tukur Yusufu Buratai, Kenyan Army Chief of Staff Lt Gen David Kipkemboi Ketter, and Benin Army Chief of Staff Maj Gen Abou Issa. Participants acknowledged progress in regional security cooperation but stressed ongoing challenges such as internal and cross-border conflicts, emphasizing that political will is crucial for effective solutions.

Following the symposium, the Chiefs of Staff of the Rwandan Armed Forces visited the Kigali Genocide Memorial to pay tribute to victims of the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi.

The symposium, themed “Enhancing Military Cooperation in Africa and Beyond,” is part of Rwanda’s broader efforts to promote continental peace, security, and military collaboration.

title: Rwanda and DRC to continue talks on FDLR dismantling and regional security
excerpt: WASHINGTON, United States - Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have agreed to reconvene next month to discuss joint security measures targeting the FDLR terrorist group, following the third meeting of…
title_en: Rwanda and DRC to continue talks on FDLR dismantling and regional security
excerpt_en: WASHINGTON, United States - Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have agreed to reconvene next month to discuss joint security measures targeting the FDLR terrorist group, following the third meeting of…
body_en:
WASHINGTON, United States - Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have agreed to reconvene next month to discuss joint security measures targeting the FDLR terrorist group, following the third meeting of the Joint Security Coordination Mechanism (JSCM) in Washington on October 21-22, 2025.

The meeting, which reviewed progress in implementing the June peace agreement, focused on strategies to dismantle the FDLR, exchange intelligence, and assess potential security challenges posed by the group. The United States Department of State reported that discussions included plans to encourage FDLR fighters to lay down their arms and be transferred to Rwanda before military operations commence to neutralize remaining threats.

The fourth JSCM meeting is scheduled for November 19-20, 2025, where representatives from both countries will evaluate progress and address emerging obstacles.

On October 10, the DRC military called on all FDLR fighters to surrender either to the Congolese government or to the United Nations peacekeeping mission (MONUSCO), a step meant to facilitate their repatriation to Rwanda. At the time of the third JSCM meeting, however, FDLR fighters had not yet complied, highlighting the ongoing challenges of implementing the peace accord.

Military operations against the FDLR are further complicated by the persistent presence of the AFC/M23 coalition in North and South Kivu provinces, where the DRC army has launched intensive strikes, including drone attacks using CH-4 unmanned aerial vehicles.

Both Kigali and Kinshasa reaffirmed their commitment to regional security, emphasizing that the dismantling of the FDLR remains a priority but will require careful coordination and sustained efforts in the coming months.

Economy and Tech.

title: Rwanda Targets Industrial Growth to Boost Exports and Strengthen Currency
excerpt: The Minister of Trade and Industry, Prudence Sebahizi, has outlined new strategies aimed at boosting Rwanda’s industrial output and reducing the trade deficit.
title_en: Rwanda Targets Industrial Growth to Boost Exports and Strengthen Currency
excerpt_en: The Minister of Trade and Industry, Prudence Sebahizi, has outlined new strategies aimed at boosting Rwanda’s industrial output and reducing the trade deficit.
body_en:
The Minister of Trade and Industry, Prudence Sebahizi, has outlined new strategies aimed at boosting Rwanda’s industrial output and reducing the trade deficit.

Speaking to the Rwanda Broadcasting Agency (RBA), Minister Sebahizi emphasized that supporting investors and closely monitoring industrial projects will be key to achieving these goals. “If we increase the productivity of our products, it reduces the gap between what we export and what we import. When that gap narrows, our currency becomes more valuable,” he said.

The minister explained that the government is prioritizing the creation of favorable conditions for investors through the establishment of industrial zones and the development of essential infrastructure such as roads, water, and electricity. “We monitor investors on a daily basis to ensure progress,” he added.

According to the Ministry of Trade and Industry, Rwanda aims to increase exports from $4.2 billion in the 2024/25 fiscal year to $4.9 billion by 2026. The country also seeks to boost industrial growth from the current 3% to 10%.

Recent data shows that Rwanda’s industrial revenue has grown from $3.3 billion to $3.4 billion. Food processing leads the manufacturing sector, accounting for 24% of output, followed by beverages and tobacco (29%), machinery and hardware (8%), textiles and leather (8%), and furniture and office equipment (7%). Minerals represent another 8% of the country’s industrial production.

Minister Sebahizi reiterated that the trade and industrial development policy will continue to focus on promoting “Made in Rwanda” products as a cornerstone of sustainable economic growth.

title: Rwanda Finalizes Master Plan to Protect Arable Land from Construction Encroachment
excerpt: The Minister of Agriculture and Livestock, Dr. Mark Cyubahiro Bagabe, has announced that Rwanda is finalizing a comprehensive master plan to regulate the use of arable land and safeguard it from illegal construction…
title_en: Rwanda Finalizes Master Plan to Protect Arable Land from Construction Encroachment
excerpt_en: The Minister of Agriculture and Livestock, Dr. Mark Cyubahiro Bagabe, has announced that Rwanda is finalizing a comprehensive master plan to regulate the use of arable land and safeguard it from illegal construction…
body_en:
The Minister of Agriculture and Livestock, Dr. Mark Cyubahiro Bagabe, has announced that Rwanda is finalizing a comprehensive master plan to regulate the use of arable land and safeguard it from illegal construction activities.

Speaking during the World Food Day celebrations held on October 24, 2025, in Nyamagabe District, Dr. Cyubahiro said the Agricultural Land Use Master Plan aims to ensure that productive farmland is preserved for agricultural purposes, preventing land depletion caused by unplanned urban expansion.

“The beauty of this master plan is that it shows where the land is and what crops will be grown on it,” he explained. “Once published in the Official Gazette, no one will be allowed to build on this land - not even for schools or football fields - because every activity will have a designated place.”

Dr. Cyubahiro noted that the plan has already met all technical and policy requirements and is awaiting formal publication before implementation, expected in November 2025 following Cabinet approval.

He admitted that delays in finalizing the framework were partly due to the Ministry’s internal processes but reaffirmed that efforts are underway to ensure its timely rollout and enforcement.

The minister also urged Rwandans to focus on maximizing productivity on the available land rather than lamenting its scarcity. “To overcome the problem of limited land, we must increase yields by using all types of fertilizers and high-quality seeds,” he said. “Some say they are expensive, but not using them is even more costly - because you’ll end up with poor harvests and less income.”

Once enacted, the master plan is expected to clearly demarcate agricultural zones and crop types across the country, strengthening Rwanda’s long-term strategy for sustainable food security and land management.
